speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
BILL in aid op provincial legislation INTRODUCED.
Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 121, to amend "An Act in said of provincial legislation (prohibiting or restricting the sale or use of intoxicating liquors."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to make certain amendments to the Act which was passed at the last .session of the House in aid of provincial legislation prohibiting or restricting the sale or use of intoxicating liquors. There are five provisions. The first is merely to reinstate in the Act a clause which was in it as it passed this House and which was struck out 'by the Senate. That clause provided that for an offence under the Act the 'party accused could be tried either at the place whence he sent the liquor in contravention of the Act, or within the province into which he sent that liquor. The Senate amended the Bill by striking out the provision permitting of a charge 'being brought against a person in the province into which the liquor was sent.
The second provision authorizes the seizure of liquors in connection with charges made of violation of the Act. The Act as it stands provides that liquor, in regard to which any such offence has been committed, may upon the conviction of the party accused, be confiscated. But if has been found in practice that the provision was defeated by reason of the disappearance of the liquor between the laying of the charge and the obtaining of the conviction. 
It is proposed that there should be power to seize the liquor and 'hold it pending the determination of the charge.
The third provision is to supplement provincial legislation prohibiting the circulation of advertising matter seeking to promote the sale of liquor. The proposed clause prohibits sending through the mails into or within any province advertising matter looking to the sale of liquor, the circulation of which is forbidden by the provincial law. Certain provinces have enacted legislation prohibiting the circulation of such literature and it was thought that it would only be proper that the post office should not carry matter in violation of a provincial law.

maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: Does that cover an advertisement in a newspaper?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: It covers any advertising circulated in any form provided the legislation of the province itself prohibits that sort of advertising. It is a general provision supplementing and protecting provincial legislation.

maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: Will this prevent an Ontario house advertising in Quebec papers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: As far as circulation in Quebec is concerned, this law would not touch it unless the provincial legislature of Quebec prohibited the circulation of such advertising. But if a province, say the province of Ontario, prohibits the circulation within the province of advertisements looking to the sale of liquor, this Act will make it an offence for any one to use the mails to send these advertisements into that province, or to use the mails for the purpose of circulating them in that province. It is following up the principle of the measure that, where a province prohibits a thing in the exercise of its power, the legislation enacted will protect that provincial legislation from being violated from an outside source.

maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: It would prevent an English or American paper, or a paper from any other province, containing an advertisement of that character, from coming into the province of Ontario without contravening the provincial law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext:
If the provincial legislature forbids the circulation of such advertising, then this law will prohibit the use of the post office to send such literature in. The next clause is introduced at the request of a large number of persons interested in temperance. It provides for

the suspension of the Scott Act wherever it is in force in counties upon the petition for an election, but without an election, in all cases where there is in force in that province legislation prohibiting the sale of liquor which in the judgment of the Governor in Council is not less restrictive than the Scott Act. This is in response to a very widely expressed desire on the part of those who are interested in the temperance movement.
Finally, there is a provision to avoid a clash which it has been pointed out exists between a provision in the Proprietary or Patent Medicines Act and the prohibitory laws of certain provinces. The Proprietary and Patent Medicines Act contains a provision imposing a penalty for the fabrication or sale, under the names of patent or proprietary medicines, of preparations containing certain quantities of alcohol. It appears that the courts have held that by reason of that provision, even though the so-called patent medicine may be clearly an alcoholic beverage, as prohibited by the provincial legislation, that clause in the Proprietary and Patent Medicines Act, the Act being Dominion legislation, superseded the provincial legislation. It is proposed by this clause, inserted in the present Bill, to enact that any of the penalties imposed by the Proprietary and Patent Medicines Act shall be in addition to, and not in substitution for, any penalty provided under provincial legislation for the sale of the same article, treating it as the sale of liquor for a beverage.

maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: What is the penalty, under that advertising section, in case a person should happen to address a paper innocently to a friend in Ontario? Would the party sending it, or the friend in Ontario receiving it, be liable?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: The penalty is not less than ten dollars and not exceeding one hundred dollars or imprisonment on any person who, by his clerk, his servant or *agent, or any person who as servant or clerk or agent, etc., sends or attempts to send through His Majesty's mail, to or from or within the province, advertising matter the circulation whereof is forbidden by the law of the province.

maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: How would you get at an American citizen who sends such matter into Canada through the mail?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SALE AND USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext:
I cannot devise any
criminal law that will apply to people in the United States. It is not within our legislative jurisdiction.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House went into committee on the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide for the appointment of a Minister of the Overseas Military Forces, a Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence, and a Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs, and that the salary of the said minister be $7,000 per annum, and that the salaries of the said Parliamentary Secretary and of the said Parliamentary Under Secretary be $5,000 per annum. The said offices to continue during the war and until the end of the session of Parliament held next after the war, or, if Parliament is sitting when the war ends, then until the end of such session of Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: The documents relating to this resolution have been laid on the Table.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: I must respectfully ask that hon. members speak a little louder. I have not heard a word uttered by the Chairman or by the minister.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I am sorry the ex-Minister of Militia has not heard what the Prime Minister stated, because he has already expressed himself on this question, and pronounced himself 'against it. There are three propositions involved in this resolution. I think, perhaps, it would have been better if they had been kept separate, instead of being bulked together. One proposition is for the creation of a second Minister of Militia, to reside in England. Another is to appoint a parliamentary under secretary for 'the Department of Militia and Defence, and the third proposition is to appoint a parliamentary under secretary for external affairs. It, provides that the salary Of the minister shall be $7,000 per annum and the salaries of the under secretaries $5,000 each. Here are three distinct motions, to create three different offices.
Let us take them separately. The proposition to create a second Minister of Militia seems to be one of very questionable wisdom. We are to have two heads of the Department of Militia, one residing in London and one residing in Ottawa. The 266
matter was discussed between the Prime Minister and the ex-Minister of Militia when the latter was in office, and the judgment of the ex-Minister of Militia, was very strongly pronounced against the creation of the second office. I believe the conclusion arrived at by my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) was absolutely correct. It is impossible for me to conceive why there should be a second head of the Militia Department. There must be confusion, there must be delay, and instead of expediting business, result must be the very reverse. We have this very day a case in point. We have had as hon. gentlemen know, a report sent in by Dr. Bruce in answer to .a report which has been before the House for a long time. Last year the ex-Minister of Militia, when he was in office very properly I believe, appointed Dr. Bruce to examine into the conditions of the military hospitals in Great Britain. Everybody remembers that just twelve months ago the newspapers were filled with complaints against the treatment of our wounded in the military hospitals of Great Britain. Although I followed the matter pretty closely at the time, I could not understand what the nature of the complaint was, but I knew, and everybody knew, that there was dissatisfaction. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia very properly tried to have the matter cleared up, and he appointed one of the most eminent surgeons in Canada, Dr. Bruce, to look into the matter. Dr. Bruce went into the ipatter very thoroughly, .and made a report. The report was not given to us in -Canada, but it was given circulation in Great Britain, and it became at once the 'Subject of very severe comment dn the press of Great Britain, for what reason it was impossible to conceive.
' Another commission was then appointed to investigate the investigation which had been made by Dr. Bruce, and so we had the Ba-btie report. That report condemns Dr. Bruce in many respects, -but it agrees with him in isveral things, and the disagreement, -after all, was only confined to one or two matters. Upon everything else the Babtie report confirmed the judgment pronounced by Dr. Bruce. The report dealt especially with what is known as .the segregation of wounded and sick in,the hospitals. Dr. Brace thought it -advisable, and rightly so, I believe, to pro-poise a review of this report. It is to be borne in mind that the committee of investigation never heard Dr. Brace, never gave him opportunity to reply, and never called upon him to give his views or -state the reasons why he had come to -his



conclusion. He was condemned ex parte. Dr. Bruce very properly, under such conditions, thought he should state his own view of the case, and. he made ia rejoinder to the report of the Babtie Committee. We have this spectacle at the present time- the report was made here to the Minister of Militia; the Minister of Militia in Ottawa sent it to the Minister of Militia in Great Britain, and so we cannot have from the Government a decision upon a matter of such moment as whether or not a report of that kind shall be communicated to Parliament. In my humble judgment, all these reports should have been communicated to Parliament without any comment at all, or without any demand 'being made for them. This is a matter which specially concerns Parliament. It cannot be said that these reports should not be communicated to Parliament because they were of such nature that their publication might be prejudicial to the service. No information detrimental to the service could be given to the enemy by these reports. The enemy could not possibly get any {information which would be serviceable in military operations from anything that iis contained in this report. All that is contained in the report is simply .a statement as to the treatment which our wounded and our sick received in the hospitals in Great Britain.
Why, therefore, is this report not communicated to Parliament? We were told the other day by the Minister of Militia that this report had been sent to Sir George Perley, the Minister of Militia Overseas, and that without the consent of Sir George Perley we cannot have it. There you have at once a conflict of authority. I understood from the Minister of Militia the other day that he had no objection to communicating the report to Parliament, but he thought that it should be sent here through Sir George Perley. Sir George Perley has it; he has been communicated with, and so far as we can gather from the answer given to-day by the Prime Minister, he has not even given an opinion as to whether this report should be submitted to Parliament. Parliament, therefore, is blocked in its work by the fact that we have a second Minister of Militia who is to-day in Great Britain.
I do not see what advantage can result from our having two heads of the Militia Department, one here and one on the other side of the ocean. The Minister of Militia is responsible to this Parliament. Another Minister of Militia, sitting in Great Britain, is responsible also to this Parlia-

ment. What control has Parliament over him? If the Department of Militia is to be properly administered, the gentleman who holds the office of minister should sit in this House. It is unheard of; it cannot conduce to good administration, to have a Minister of Militia who does not sit in this House. The gentleman who administers the Department of Militia, or any other department, should be a member of the Senate or of the House of Commons, sitting each day in his place, ready at all times to give information and to account for the business with which he is entrusted. I may he told: you must have somebody in England to look after militia affairs. Certainly, you must. The gentleman who should be in England to represent the Militia Department should be an officer of that department, responsible directly to the Minister of Militia, who, in turn, is responsibly to Parliament. Take the case of the administration of the fighting forces in Europe. The general in charge of the British army fighting in France is responsible to a minister, who is responsible to Parliament. A condemnation of this new proposal of my right hon. friend is found in the fact that we have two' ministers of the Department of Militia, one here, from whom we can get no information and answers to any questions that may he put, and one in England, from whom we cannot get information in relation to a matter of such moment as that to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
The right hon. (gentleman continually comes back to the report of Dr. Bruce, whatever subject may be under discussion by Parliament. He entirely overlooks the fact that since Colonel Bruce's report was made there has been an entire reorganization of the army medical service overseas. That service is now under the direct control of General Foster, of whom I spoke yesterday. General Foster is the Director of Medical Service so far as the Canadian Expeditionary Force in Great Britain and France is concerned. The management, therefore, which was the subject (of Colonel Bruce's report and animadversion has been changed in the meantime, and I have not heard any criticism of the management or administration of General Foster since he took charge. So far as the comment of Colonel Bruce is concerned, I have explained over and over again that in the ordinary course it should have gone to the Minister of Overseas Service, 'because it related to matters which are under his

jurisdiction. The jurisdiction is not common to the Minister of Militia and Defence and the Minister of Overseas Service. The jurisdiction was divided, just as in Great Britain the ministry of munitions took over part of that jurisdiction which had previously been exercised by the Secretary of State for War, and just as the ministry of shipping in Great Britain has taken over part of the jurisdiction formerly appertaining to another department.
I could name twelve, fourteen, perhaps twenty different instances in Great Britain where a part of the jurisdiction of one department was transferred to another department, for the very simple reason that the exigencies of the war demanded it.
Mr. MARCH,: Do these new ministers sit in the British House of Commons?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: I think that nearly all are members of the House, but they do not pretend to sit in the House all the time. Sir George Perley is a member of this House. He cannot be here and at the same time attend to his duties overseas; questions have to be answered here on his behalf. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) informs me that Sir Joseph Maclay, Minister of Shipping, is not a member of Parliament in Great Britain. Sir Joseph Maclay has direction of all matters respecting the providing of shipping. He directs where it shall be employed; whether it shall be employed on the Atlantic or on the Pacific; whether it can be most usefully employed in transportation between Great Britain and Australia and New Zealand, between Great Britain and Canada and the United States, or between Great Britain and Argentine. He has under his direction the building of additional shipping, not only in Great Britain, but in all parts of the world. He has an exceedingly important jurisdiction. One of our last duties in our recent visit to Great Britain was to confer with him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: He does not sit in Parliament, but he must be responsible to some minister who does sit in Parliament. He cannot be independent; I am sure of that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
So far as that is concerned, Sir George Perley, as I have already mentioned, is a member of and is responsible to this Parliament.
Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, although a member of Parliament, does not attend all the sittings of Parliament. He goes there only on very exceptional occa-

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I beg my
right hon. friend's pardon. An arrangement, was made under which Mr. Bonar Law, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, was appointed leader in the House of Commons,, with the direct intention, which has been carried out very fully, that the leader of the Government should not be burdened with parliamentary duties, but that he should direct the whole of his time and energies to matters concerned with the' carrying on of the war. He does go there on important occasions, but very rarely indeed. While we were in Great Britain, during more than two months I do not think that he went to the House of Commons half a dozen times. The leadership of the House' of Commons is carried on by Mr. Bonar Law, not by the leader of the Government.
As far as the remaining criticism of my right hon. friend is concerned, I do not know that it calls for any answer at the present time. The duties which have been imposed upon the Minister of Overseas service are very considerable; his jurisdiction is complete with regard to the troops that are overseas. He reports to Council through the Prime Minister; the reports that he makes are submitted to the Minister of Militia and Defence in order that Council may have the benefit of the suggestions of the Minister of Militia and Defence with regard to any recommendations so made. There has been no friction; there has been no difficulty, so far as I am aware, and I think the system has worked out very well-

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: What as the object of having ,a Minister of Militia and Defence overseas? The Overseas Minister must report to the ^minister here so that his recommendations may reach, Council. Why would not a deputy minister in England responsible to the Minister of Militia here serve the purpose?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: It is true that he does not happen to be here. But the 2664

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend states that a Minister of Shipping has been appointed in England. I am not aware of the circumstances of this
new.-

creation. There may 'be suidh am officer [DOT]there, but I am satisfied that it he is not a /member of one branch or the other oi the British Parliament, he is serving under a minister who is responsible to Parliament, who sits in Parliament and answers for .him. Without knowing the circumstances,
1 am satisfied of that. My right hon. friend is surely not serious in comparing the position of Sir George Parley .as Minister of Militia overseas with that of Mr. Lloyd George, Prime Minister of England. When Mr. Lloyd George became Prime Minister and reorganized the Government, he divested himself of many of the duties which hitherto appertained to the Premiership. He has not undertaken to lead the House hknself, having handed over that duty to Mr. Bonar Law, who is to-day the leader of the House .and who attends to .all the business of the House, .because some member of the Government must be in the House to look after the business of the House generally, 'and, if needs be, to support before the House the policies of the Government. Although Mr. Lloyd George has to ia large extent divested himself of the burdens .appertaining ordinarily to the Premiership of Great Britain, .still he is the Prime Minister .and a member of the British House of Commons, and when some great occasion .arises he comes to Parliament to explain the policy of the Government and to lead the House. Is my right hon. friend going to compare Mr. Lloyd George's position with that of Sir George Perley? It is true .that Sir George Perley has been elected a member of this House, and that he can sit here at 'any time, but for all the practical purposes of his appointment as Minister of Militia overseas, he does not sit in this House, and under those circumstances there would be confusion. This appointment, so for from working with advantage, would, I think, work with great disadvantage, .and a better way would be to make the position the same as that of the new 'Minister of Shipping, Mr. Macluy, who serves under a minister who is responsible for him in the British House of Commons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I do not understand why my right hon. friend attributes to my remarks some meaning which I did not at all intend to convey. I understood my right hon. friend to raise the objection that Sir George Perley was not here to answer questions. In reply I pointed out to him that even a gentleman so directly responsible as the Prime Minister of the 
United Kingdom has found it necessary, for the purposes of this war, to divest himself almost wholly of his parliamentary duties and to hand those duties over to another member of Parliament. I was drawing the conclusion that, under our present conditions a minister of the overseas forces should stay at his post in Great Britain and devote himself to his duties there instead of coming here to discharge duties in this House. I was not comparing their relative positions. I was .comparing the two facts that in both cases there was urgent need; in the one case that the Prime Minister should relieve himself of his' parliamentary duties, .and in the otheT case, as we think, that the .Minister of Overseas Service should devote himself to his duties on the spot in Great Britain and not cross the seas, leaving those duties to take care of themselves, and sit in this House to answer questions.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.

speechtext:
Would the Prime
Minister explain to the House what the functions of the overseas Minister of Militia may. be, what those of the Minister of Militia in Canada may be, wherein they harmonize, and wherein they clash?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.

He assumes a part of the jurisdiction formerly exercised by the Minister of Militia and Defence. He assumes in respect of the Canadian forces overseas the duties which had. been previously exercised in respect of that force by the Minister of Militia and Defence.

speechtext:
If Sir George Perley is
to receive a /salary from the day of his appointment, he will be violating the independence o.f Parliament Act because, having accepted an office of emolument under the Crown, he .should vacate his seat in this House and return to his constituents to seek re-election. Does the salary date from the date of his appointment or from the date of the closing of this House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: The point raised by my hon. friend is provided for in the Bill to be founded on this resolution, and we have in regard to it numerous precedents in Great Britain since the war began.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: Are there precedents in the cases of the other two appointments?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I have no objection whatever to the portion of this resolution

referring to the Parliamentary Secretary for Militia and the Parliamentary Undersecretary for External Affairs, and I shall be only too pleased to assist in the passing of the resolution as regards them. Their appointment is a very good idea.
I object, however, to the appointment of a Minister of the Overseas Military Forces, to be stationed in England, not only on the ground of the administrative character of the office, but on the ground of the manner in which it is being conducted. In the first place, we have the fact that although the second Bruce report in answer to the Babtie report has not yet been laid on the table of the House, we have a commentary upon it published yesterday in England by Sir George Perley. This report should be withheld until this House is in possession of it. From Sir George Perley's admissions yesterday, we have for the first time a clear idea of what the Militia Department has been up against so far as that gentleman as High Commissioner is concerned. From the outset of this war, Sir George Perley has taken the stand that Canada is in the position of a Crown colony and that we should have no right, nor recognition, nor control, over our troops beyond the seas, other than what may be accorded to us by the British War Office. Since 1914, Sir George Perley took the position that I, as Minister of Militia of Canada, had nothing whatever to say or to do in connection with the troops in England, and that any arrangements from a military viewpoint were absolutely under the control of the British War Office. The letting of contracts, purchases for the troops, the establishment of the V.A.D. hospitals and matters of that kind, of course, would be arranged, as they evidently, according to the report published yesterday, have been arranged, through Sir George Perley's influence with the British authorities.
The findings of the Bruce report of a year ago have been more than justified by reason of the fact that the V.A.D. hospitals in England are being practically wiped out to-day by the British medical authorities themselves. In fact, they are no longer in existence, orders having been issued that they are all to be congregated together and run as proper hospitals. I think the statement has been made that they will contain not less than 500 beds in place of the small number they used to contain, and I understand that the control is to be entirely different. As I have said, I have no objection whatever to this resolution, provided the Department of Militia overseas is left
under the control of the Department of Militia in this country. There is no use shutting our eyes to the facts. There is not a member of this House who has had dealings with the Militia Department since Sir Edward Kemp took control who has not felt sorry for that gentleman on account of the humiliating position which he has been obliged to take again and again in connection with military matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.

speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
He has no say in these matters. I understand that he has been reprimanded repeatedly for presuming to ask certain questions of those in control across the sea. He bears it all with very good grace, but there is not one of us who has not realized the humiliating position in which he has been placed. I would sometimes write a letter to the department fpr some mother asking for information about her son, and would receive a printed reply saying, "We understand from Sir George Perley's Office that so and so," and I would be told to proceed under such and such a section of the Act, and in the course of a year or two I might get the desired information.
But apart from the personal element, there is also this fact:	Officers sail from
this country under pay, under discipline, under an allowance and under the administration of the Department of Militia in this country, but when they get to the other side they are subjected to an entirely different set of conditions. For instance, the Minister of Militia here, no matter what his knowledge of an officer may be, has no say in promoting him once he gets across the water. There is another very .serious objection-I am giving these objections very briefly-and that is the tremendous expense involved. The statement is made that whereas General Carson administered the whole of Canada's war department in England with less than 50 men, and did it well, despite the fact that Sir George Perley attempted to thwart -him at every turn by interfering, there are now 1,200 to 4 p.m. 1,500 men, not counting the pay officers, doing the work of the Adjutant General's office and other offices. In fact, I understand that only about 30 men were employed by General Carson for this work. I challenge any member of this House whc has taken a battalion overseas to stand up in his place and say that he has received satisfactory treatment from the Overseas Militia Office in England.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I don't know anything about that. They aTe under the Militia Department, but I cannot say whether their appointments are civil or military.
I certainly cannot see why the Bruce report in answer to the Babtie charges has not been published; but that is neither here nor there. As it has not been published, I certainly think it was a strange proceeding on the part of Sir George Perley to seek to answer it in advance in the press of England yesterday. I will not

say that his statement was given to his subsidized press, who have been sending out a continual stream of reports from his office during the last three years on lines suitable to him, but his statement was certainly calculated to prejudice public opinion in advance of the publication of the Bruce report after Parliament has been prorogued. Under all the circumstances, I think that that part of the resolution referring to Sir George Perley's salary should be withheld until the Bruce report is published.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
The blame will have to lie where it belongs, if it is a document of the character described by my hon. friend. It was really prepared, ! think, for the purpose of giving certain information and suggestions in a convenient form, as the inquiries were very numerous.
I do not find that the press despatch in the Montreal Gazette contains any reply to Colonel Bruce's report. There is a reference to what Colonel Bruce's report contains, but the comments upon it are not set forth in the despatch in the slightest degree.
As to the number of men employed overseas in connection with the administration of the forces in England, I should be greatly surprised if the number exceeds the number employed under the administration of my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes). I cannot speak positively as to that, because I have never made any computation, but I know that most of the men at the head of departments over there are men An whom my hon. friend had a great deal of confidence. There is Colonel McRae, for instance, who was at the head of the Quartermaster General's Department under the administration of my hon. friend. He has proved himself very capable, and is still at the head of that department. Colonel Ross, who is at the head of the Pay Department, and is a very capable man, was also selected by my hon. friend. Colonel Foster had a long record in the permanent force, and was regarded by my hon. friend as a man worthy of an important position. I do not think he filled

his present position under my hon. friend's administration, but I understand that ne filled some position of importance in France. Colonel Thacker, I think, retains practically the same position he had before, that of Adjutant General. As regards General Turner, who is the head of the military organization in England, I think it is universally agreed that in the discharge of his new duties he has proved himself very diligent and very efficient. These, I think, are the most important changes that have been made.
There really has not been any friction in carrying out the work of the two departments. They co-operate with each other very harmoniously. There are doubtless suggestions from one department to the other from time to time, but there has been no friction, and no difficulty.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
That fly-sheet, I understand, wias prepared in England, or at least it is very similar to one that was in use in England. I do not know 'whether the Minister of Militia for Canada is anxious to claim the fatherhood of the thing or not, but I take the ground-I have taken it for a quarter of a century, and I shall take it for -a quarter of a century more-that with all due regard to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), and the proposition he has made to-day, I will not communicate with (the Minister of Militia, or with any other gentleman occupying the position of minister, 'through any subordinate on matters affecting my constituency, or any of my constituents. The proper plan, When any member has anything to do with any department, is to notify the minister of the department. I notify the Minister of Militia and get back in return this notice: "You will be kind enough to read this over and see which section refers to the case in point; then notify your friend in the country that she is to apply to the P. W. X. Y. officer in her district, who will in turn report the matter to the Militia Department here; in due time it will reach England and France, and in the course of the next quarter of a century or more a reply will come back. That is not the manner in which things were done when I was in charge of the department. I recognized members of Parliament had the right to come to me and ask me questions, and I, as Minister of Militia, looked after these things and saw that their requests were properly attended to, and as far as we could we gave them the data. I could give an instance to this House where a mother had tried for over two months to find out what
had happened to her son. I aim not blaming the present Minister of Militia, because he had nothing to do with it, although he is taking the blame as a gentleman and trying to look happy. Finally, that poor mother appealed to me. Through the sources of information which I had, I found out in less than two days that her son was dead and had been buried in France last January, he having been wounded in the latter part of November. Three weeks after that mother had received my message, she received-I do not blame this ofiice here-an intimation from that concern in London that this young man was dangerously ill at a hospital in France, when, as ai matter of fact, her poor boy was dead and buried on the 5th of January. The mother again appealed to me, and upon making further inquiries the information which I had received was verified. I am merely pointing out what this system does. It is bureaucracy, and it is against proper administration and action. That is the only point I am making in regard to the matter. As to the officers in London, I venture to say that the number is twenty times as great as it was formerly. I am not speaking of the senior officers. They could not get rid of a good many of the senior officers over there if they tried.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: In which department has there been an increase?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
In the Adjutant
General's department -and in others. I do not know how they employ all the men there are to he found in the Argyle building. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister was over there and he saw them. There are six buildings filled with these gentlemen, whereas General Carson had only fifty and that included the clerical service and the Quarter-master General's staff.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: Are these gentlemen civilians or soldiers? If they are soldiers why do they not go to the front?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I do not know, but I understand they ore mostly soldiers. I would suggest to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that he might inquire as to the number of men who are employed in that building alone. The information I have is largely obtained from gentlemen of high standing who have been over there, and who have returned to Canada, as well as some officers who have returned. I have not made any enumeration whatever, as I did not think it was part of my function to

do so. I have assisted the minister in Canada in every legitimate way, and I have retrained from meddling in the work at all. But my information is that there are six buildings full of gentlemen in London doing the work which was formerly done by General Carson and his fifty men. I would ask any officer in the minister's department to speak up. frankly and say how the thing is going. The department here has been wiped out of existence in so far .as control of the Record office work or any other work is concerned. I believe that a change has come about in the last few months whereby Canada is recognized to a certain extent as being entitled to her rights. But all the service that I can find that Sir George Perley was rendering to this country was simply putting obstacles in the way .and in bringing these V.A.D. hospitals under the patronage of some distinguished people in England, and in that way making them appendages to the British machine, rather than independent entities under the direction of the great nation which Canada is to-day.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
Why should not an under-secretary of the Militia Department, for instance, relieve the minister of a great deal of work?
M.r. LEMIEUX: Le<t us take the .undersecretary of External Affairs, and I say, without fear of being contradicted, that, with the Prime Minister as head of that branch of the service and with Sir Joseph Pope, who works night and day for his country, who attends to his duty as no other officials in the Government attend to their duties, an under-secretary is not needed-unless it is to prepare campaign literature. I do not say that the hon. gentleman-dioos that, but I repeat that, with Sir Joseph Pope at the head of the department, no under-secretary is needed, and nobody in Ottawa will believe he is needed. My hon. friend says: What about the Department of Militia? If he will accept that bouquet from me, I will say that, as long as the hon. member (Sir Sam Hughes) was at the head of the Militia Department, the hon. member for Shelburne was not needed as under-secretary. The ex-minister could do his work and do it well.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: I must say that I would have been only too delighted, and was delighted after he was appointed, to have the services of this worthy member. He was certainly of great assistance to me in the department.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
Coming back to Sir
George Perley, I say that the new office of Overseas Minister is not at all needed. We have the right to appoint a High Commissioner din London, -and if a successor to Lord Strathcona bad been appointed four or five years ago, the High 'Commissioner for Canada in London to-diay would not have needed by his side an Overseas Minister. Australia is playing its part, in the present war; New Zealand also; hot I do not know that any Overseas Ministers nave been appointed for those two Dominions. For what reason is Sir George Perley put in that position? The High Commissioner for Canada should be the channel of communication -between' the British authorities, the Canadian general, the Canadian troopis. land the Canadian Government. For my part, I do not want to see the day when a 'Canadian minister will be residing in London. I want to -see the Can-adian ministers in the Canadian House of Commons, -and not in London. They are responsible to Canada and to Canada only, and I am glad to find my bon. friend (Sir Sam- Hughes) taking the stand that the Minister of Militia is primarily responsible to the Parliament of Canada and to the Canadian people. The atmosphere of London is uncongenial to some of our Canadian statesmen. Not very long ago, I read in the Canadian Courier of Toronto the following, on the subject of Canadian autonomy:
Sir Robert is imperialistic. Autonomy is rapidly disappearing and, ominously, the losses are being outrun by imperialistic phraseology. Sir Robert declares that he is a member of "The Imperial War Cabinet,*' although there is no such thing. He has agreed that Canadian resources shall be considered "Empire resources'* and Canadian assets. "Imperial assets." He has agreed to "concerted action" in the development of "the Empire's resources," and to the establishment of an "Imperial Development Board" to <ie-vise methods, to advise and to guide. He has agreed to the creation of the "Imperial Mineral Resources Bureau" to consider how our resources may he "made available to meet the total requirements of the Empire." He has bound up our economic interests with all parts of the King's dominions. He has associated us with all the Allies in a "common economic policy," as against all outsiders, including the United States. Sir Starr Jameson's Committee proposes making Imperial profit out of our lands. The Earl of Dunraven declares that our fisheries "must be viewed as an Imperial
not as a local asset." Sir Robert agrees that "our natural resources ought to be conserved for the general national benefit." Canada has ceased to he autonomous. She has become a British sphere of influence.
Whilst I do not object to Canada being
a British sphere of influence in the broad, sense, I much prefer to have her one of the Overseas Dominions, possessing her full 'autonomy and living n-p to the precedents and the principles which are laid down in the British constitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I wish to refer to only one phase of the discussion and that is in regard to what has been described as a fly sheet.
I object to this document which I hold in my hand, a circular letter dated February 11, 1917, and for which I am responsible, being called by such an undignified name. It has been found that the more troops we send overseas and the more that arrived in France and the more casualties that occurred, the more inquiries reach the department from the relatives of the soldiers.
That is qnitS natural, and as the inquiries have increased in number, running sometimes into thousands a day, we have endeavoured to classify them. After careful study we classified them under ten different heads, -and1 I think we have pretty nearly covered the %round. It is impossible for the Minister of Militia to personally see .all the friends -and relatives who make these requests, and i-t is impossible for the Minister of Militia to conduct -all the correspondence in connection with them. Nevertheless ia letter is -dictated' -and -sent to every relative and friend of the soldier at the front, or in England or in Canada, who makes inquiry. On the 1st February, 1917, we embodied these requests under ten different headings, -and I shall take up a moment of the time of the House to read whiat was intended by the issue of this circular. I think the committee will agree with me that -such .action was necessary. In fact, I may say that the circular which I bold in my band was found to be so popular that we have had several different editions printed since that time, and have had them circulated amongst members of provincial legislatures!, members of Parliament, members of the Government, the judges, and prominent people from one end of the Dominion to the other. These circulars have done great service in- giving information in respect to the conditions and the surroundings of soldiers with respect to whom requests were made that they should he sent out to Canada on furlough.

The circular reads:
Department of Militia and Defence Canada.
Memorandum Regarding Methods of Dealing
With Personal Requests Concerning Soldiers Serving Overseas With the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
A large number of requests of a personal nature with reference to soldiers serving overseas with the Canadian Expeditionary Force are daily received by this department and by the Canadian military authorities in England. It is, therefore, considered desirable to explain the methods which, in the interests of fair and equitable treatment to all concerned, are followed in each case.
The policy adopted with respect to these requests has been formulated with every possible regard for the personal interests of the soldiers concerned and the natural anxiety and interest on their behalf of their relatives and friends. It should be remembered, however, that, at this stage of the war the brave men of our own Canadian army and those of the British and Allied armies require all the support that can be given them in their heroic fight for liberty, justice and civilization. To this end the services of every available man in whatever capacity his physical and other capabilities fit him to occupy are urgently required both in England and at the front. It should, therefore, be clearly understood that the exigencies of the military situation must be the primary consideration in dealing with such requests.
The following statement explains the procedure adopted in dealing with the various cases mentioned.
A. E. Kemp,
Minister of Militia and Defence.
Ottawa, February 1, 1917.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has made a statement which will go from one end of this country to the other, and appear as an uncontradicted statement, to the effect that the newly-created office of Under-Secretary for External Affairs was for campaign purposes. Surely it must be patent to anybody that such a charge against the integrity of this Government is an exceedingly serious one. If either ought to be backed up or withdrawn, and it most distinctly ought to be promptly contradicted. The people of this country are more than alive to charges of any description, particularly at this time, and I cannot rest content without protest, if such a charge as this, made by a distinguished front bencher of the Opposition, is not at least disputed, or, in some way, required to be confirmed. The hon. gentleman from Rouville knows perfectly well that what he said will go with tremendous weight to the people of this country. An election is impending. The justification for the creation of the position has not been set out; no doubt it will be. The salary, I am free to confess, being $7,500 a year-that is the Sessional indemnity and the salary-is to my mind excessive at this time. I will vote for it, because we are on the eve of an election.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: I feel that we have got to vote for it.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: You want all you can get.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I think it is too much.
I am willing to go it blind and vote for it, but I am not willing to go it blind with a charge uncontradicted, like that made by the hon. gentleman from Rouville. That statement is ian .absolute insult to this House, if it is not true, and if it is not true it most distinctly requires explanation of the most serious kind. If we can sit in this House and listen to charges of that

kind and they do not disturb our equanimity, we are on the 'brink of a moral catastrophe, to put it mildly. I do not wonder the people .are shocked -at partyism and partisanship, which applies, of course, to. both parties. I cannot resume my seat without reiterating the statement that such a charge as that should Ibe promptly withdrawn as an ignominious exaggeration, made for party purposes at an opportune time, without one tittle of proof or reason, or that it should be substantiated. I hear nothing from the hon. gentleman from Rou-ville during the course of my humble remarks to indicate that he has the slightest intention of taking it back. If is a very ts-ad commentary, indeed, upon the state of affairs in this 'Country, if such a statement can be made with impunity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I doubt very much whether the language which has fallen from the hon. gentleman from Rou-ville (Mt. Lemieux) will produce anything like the impression which my hon. friend from Peterborough seems to imagine. We hear very often from the hon. gentleman from Renville in a somewhat exaggerated way.
I do not know that any one takes his remarks very seriously. As a matter of fact, he is profoundly ignorant of the subject which he undertook to discuss. I know what the duties of the Prime Minister as Secretary of State for External Affairs have been during the past two or three years. I know those duties better, perhaps, than any other hon. member of the House, and I venture to say that they have been twenty times as great as they were under normal conditions. The correspondence with the Mother Country, on matters frequently of the greatest importance, has been as much in a month as under ordinary conditions it would be in a year; I believe that I am understating the fact in that respect. The Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs has been occupied with the duties of his office during very long hours. He has rendered very important assistance; he has done good work, relieving me from very many matters which previously occupied my attention. My only regret is that I did not take steps early in the war to have an Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs appointed; it would have been better for the interests of the country had I done so. I would have had more time to give to general considerations; my attention would not have been eo much taken up with matters which, though important, were nevertheless of a
somewhat routine character. As to the necessity that Parliamentary secretaries in Great Britain should -go back to their constituents, on their appointment, the hon. member is -as bal-dy informed as about other matters of which he has spoken. If he had seen fit to inform himself before speaking, he would have known that when the Government of the United Kingdom was reconstituted nearly a year ago, an Act was passed which made it unnecessary for the members taking office to he elected again to Parliament. The period over which that law took effect was two or three months, a sufficient length of time to enable the Government to be reorganized and the ministers to assume their duties. We are doing on a very small scale indeed in respect of these three gentlemen what was done in Great Britain in December and January last on a very large scale. When my hon. friend speaks of British precedent, he puts the best possible argument into my -mouth because- I need -only refer to British precedent to establish thoroughly the position which I have taken. It is perfectly true that Mr. Churchill had an election- recently in Dundee. I am speaking, how-eve-r, o-f the period when the British Government was reorganized, a period of two or three months, over which the statute to which I allude extended The statute ceased hi have operation after the time mentioned; in the meantime, the Government had been reorganized. I am citing that as an instance where, upon a very large scale indeed, Parliament made provision for members accepting offices of emolument under the Crown without the necessity of being returned again as members of Parliament.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.

speechtext:
It dates from the time he commenced to discharge his duties. I have already explained that Sir George Perley has written a letter to me in which he expresses a desire not to receive any salary. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has made remarks with regard to Sir George Perley that I think are not in very good taste. For six years Sir George Perley -has discharged the duties of a minister of the Crown without any remuneration whatever. During that time he has continually undertaken the discharge of duties for other ministers, sometimes for three, four or five months at a time. He has worked hard and inde-

fatigably in the discharge of the duties so confided to him, sometimes during the long summer months administering here in Ottawa three or four departments when the heads of those departments were taking needed rest. I venture to say that he has given more service to the people of this country without remuneration than a dozen like the member for Rouville ever did or are ever likely to. He has discharged the duties of High Commissioner for three years in London without any remuneration whatever. I think, therefore, that it is perhaps not in the best taste to comment in 'the tone which my hon. friend from' Rouville saw fit to assume with regard to the salary which I now propose to ask Parliament to vote for that office.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend has said that the remarks of the member for Rouville were not in the best of taste; I would suggest that my right hon. friend's remarks in 'answer to the member ifor Rouville are far from being in the best of taste. The member for Rouville had good reason $o speak as he did; he showed that he knew as much about the subject with -which he was dealing as my right hon. friend did. Last year, or the year before, when the British Government was reorganized, a special Act was passed for a special occasion, dispensing with the necessity of the ministers going before their electors before accepting office. But this Act was only temporary, and they have now reverted to the old practice of requiring a member of the House of Commons to go before his electors before accepting an office of emolument under the Crown. The latest instance of this was the election of Mr. Churchill. In this respect, therefore, my hon, friend (Mr. Lemieux) was well 'advised in speaking as be did. I think that we had better approach the discussion of this matter not with our tempers, but with frankness 'and as 'becomes members of Parliament. I am prepared to believe what my right bon. friend says with regard to the work of the Department of External Affairs. I knew the work when I was in office, and I am sure that during the war it has increased immensely. That the inside work has increased, -and that the member for North Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark)- with whom nobody has any quarrel; whom everybody in this House respects-has done <a good deal to relieve the Prime Minister of the discharge of duties which would otherwise have fallen upon him, I am prepared to believe. But in what respect has

the Prime Minister been relieved upon the floor of this House by the member for North Bruce? Whatever the member for North Bruce 'may have done in his office, so far as the work of this House is concerned he has not earned the salary which it is proposed to give him os Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State. Whether or not he is entitled to the secretaryship we need not diiscuss now; we will come to that when the second reading of the Bill is reached.
With regard to the Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence, I say the same; I leave it to every man in this committee whether he has been of any assistance to the Minister of Militia. The member for Rouville referred to the *work done by Sir Joseph Pope. Sir Joseph Pope is a very good officer; he may have equals, but certainly he has no superior in activity, energy, integrity and all the qualities required of one in his position. If he requires a larger staff, it is proper that he should get it. However, we will defer the discussion of these matters until we reach the second reading of the Bill.

I rise only to

Not confined.

speechtext:
I did not say so.
iSir ROBERT BORDEN: If they are not confined to that, then my hon. friend's argument falls absolutely to the ground. Does he mean to say that Sir George Murray suggested the appointment of undersecretaries in this country merely for the purpose of having them answer questions in Parliament? Any such idea as that is out of the question. They were suggested for the purpose of relieving, to a certain extent, the ministers in discharge of their official duties, not only in Parliament, but in respect to the work of their office. The work of the office is much more burdensome and serious than the work in Parliament, because the former extends throughout all the year. So fax as that is concerned, the new under secretaries may not, up to the present time, have taken up a very large share of the work in Parliament. They 'are

new to the duties of their office, and it is *beyond question that in other sessions they will, more and more, assume a .larger share of parliamentary duties in addition to the work which they perform in connection with office routine.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I do not resent what my Tight hon. friend has stated in regard to the remarks I made, but I would like to know from him what he finds in those remarks which is out of taste concerning Sir George Perley. I have said nothing against Sir George Perley. He is a personal friend1 of mine, but if Sir George Perley chooses to be High .Commissioner for Canada in London, as there is a salary attaching to that function, let him resign as a member of the Government and then let him accept that position, and nobody will find fault with him. But if he chooses to be acting High Commissioner in London and at the same time be overseas Minister of Militia and Defence, to accept emo.uniont as snch and. not seek re-election, I say, as a Canadian, and as a .student of British institutions 'and the Canadian constitution, that /Sir George Perley is evading one of the cardinal principles of onr Canadian constitution and of the British institution. I cited the example of Mr. Churchill, who is just as important a man in the British Government as Sir George Per.ey is in the .Oanadian Government. Mr. Churchill has had, for a young man, a long and brilliant career in public life, and yet when he is called upon by his Sovereign to join the British Government, he resigns his .seat; he goes before his electors in Dundee; he gets re-elected, and he joins the Government and can receive the emoluments of office. By what divine Tight should Sir George Perley-who, it is true, has been acting High Commissioner in London without any emolument, but on whose head honours have been showered, he has been knighted for that very object-now join the Government, receive emolument and not seek re-election from the farmers of the county of Argenteuil? He must not expect the electors of Argenteuil to look upon him as their representative in the Government if he does not adhere to the principles of the Canadian constitution. By what right, I repeat, can Sir George Perley (after having been away from Canada for five years), become a minister of tlie Crown and not seek re-election from his electors in the county of Argenteuil? High as is Sir George Perley, knighted as he may be, I say that the plain farmer,
Mr. McGibbon, who is a candidate against him in Argenteuil, will defeat him to-morrow if he runs in that county.

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I object to there being two Ministers of Militia both on account of the dual control and on constitutional grounds. What we should have in England is an officer responsible to the Minister of Militia or some other member of the Government here, but that officer should not have ministerial functions. What has happened shows that my contention is justified. We should have some officer who will be in a position similar to that of General Carson. Let Sir George Perley be responsible to the Minister of Militia here.
Mr. LEMIEUX- And responsible to his electors here.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: That goes without saying.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: Not according to the Prime Minister.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I would not have a *minister in England at all, so that the officer appointed would not require to be responsible to .any electors. The manner in which the appointment is provided for in the Bill would place in the hands of the party in power an autocratic authority that should not be exercised by any Government, and it would have .a .tendency to take away from the people certain rights, which, under the constitutipn, they 'are entitled to exercise.
The Minister of Militia in Canada does not understand my objection to his circular. If my recollection serves me aright, the first circular that came out distinctly

stated that Sir George Perley objected to being troubled with those letters. He objected to having those questions asked of him. The poor people throughout the length and breadth of the country do not know that the country is divided into military districts, and who these red tab and brass tab people in the Militia Departments are. I understood that the people' were not posted on 'the petty details of the department, and when a mother from any part of the Dominion wrote a letter to the department, I instructed that it be handed to a clerk who had as many brains and as much capacity to act as any red tab officer in London, Kingston, Toronto, or other military district. Whenever a member of Parliament came into the department the instructions were that he was to be shown into my room alt once; that when he sent a communication, that communication was to be acted on as though it was an order from the people's representative, and we did what we could to meet the people's wishes, eo that any request which a member made, even although it was in regard to a poor, common soldier, should be looked after immediately. The reason I take exception to this appointment is that this is not meeting the people's representatives with the dignity, the courtesy &nd the business treatment to which they are entitled. Let me give a specific instance. A poor woman from London, Ontario, wrote to the Minister of Militia, asking some questions. An officer under the minister here sent the letter hack to her with, one of these circulars, telling her to read the circular and to apply under the proper heading. She did not know to whom she should apply. She did not know that London was a military district, although she lived in London. That is only one instance out of tens of thousands throughout the country. I took the case up and put it through for her myself.
The point I want to impress upon the Minister of Militia is that members of Par1 lament, in making requests or asking for information from the minister, should not be placed in the same position as an unofficial cit'/.en, but should be treated with that courtesy and dignity to which a member of Parliament is entitled. So far as the under-secretaries are concerned, I think they can be of very great service, especially during war time, and I purpose with all my heart supporting that section of the resolution. But as regards the otfier part of the resolution, it is constitutionally wrong, it is wrong from the standpoint of our success in the war, and it is wrong fSir Sam Hughes.]
upon a great many other grounds that I do not care to enter into here to-day.

speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister what authority, if any, the Minister of Militia here will have over the Minister of Militia in England, and if he has none, to whom is the Minister of Militia in England responsible? Would that necessarily follow, simply because a copy of his re-

port was sent to the Minister of Militia and Defence?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.

It has been
found to follow. My hon. friend will understand that the duties of the Minister of Militia Overseas are concerned with the expeditionary force in Great Britain and France. maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: I wish to add that I have written a great many letters to the Militia Department since the war started, and have received nothing but courteous treatment.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: The Prime Minister states that the Minister of Militia Overseas is responsible, just as is any other minister of the Crown. But there is this difference. Suppose the Minister of Public Works, for instance were to build one story of a building, and another minister then took charge and put up a second story and furnished the building. That is analagous to what it is proposed to do here. The Minister of Militia in Canada does a certain portion of the work; he arranges for the letting of contracts, gets all the equipment ready, makes appointments and promotions, and the troops are then sent over to the Old Country and put under entirely different management. We should have the same control, the same exercise of administrative authority and discipline over our troops in England as we have in Canada, but we have not got that to-day. I do not propose going into that just now, but I am prepared to go into it if necessary.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I do not wish to say any-ting against Sir George Perley, because I have had the pleasure of his acquaintance for several years. He has been 5 p.m. an active and successful business man, we must admit, but he has certainly undertaken to do too much during the war. If he had remained content with being a member of Parliament, and a member of the present Administration, and devoted himself to the duties devolving upon him in connection therewith, he would have not been criticised. But in addition to those duties he has undertaken the work of the High Commissioner, and on top of this, it is now proposed to make him Overseas Minister of Militia. On the formation of the present Administration five Cabinet seats were allotted to the province of Quebec. One was the minister now under discussion, without portfolio; the others were the Minister of Justice, the Postmaster General, the Minister of Inland Revenue, and the Secretary of State. The result is that to-day the Minister of Justice is .administering his own department and the Post Office Department, and the Minister of Inland Revenue is administering his own department and the Department of Secretary of State. Hon. Mr. Blondin being on active service, and Mr. Patenaude having resigned, the province of Quebec finds itself with but two representatives in the Cabinet. What would the people of Ontario think if Ontario had only two representatives in the Cabinet?
I think a word should also be said for the electors of Argenteuil. Sir George Perley-he was plain Mr. Perley then-was given a seat in the Cabinet on being elected by a large majority for the county of Argenteuil. Being an English Protestant, and representing one of the thirteen Protestant constituencies in the province of Quebec, he became by that fact a representative of the Protestant minority in the province of Quebec. We have always had such representative in every Cabinet. But since Sir George Perley went to England the Protestant minority of Quebec has been without a representative in the Cabinet, and the electors of Argenteuil without a representative in this House. We are now asked to vote a salary to Sir George Perley and make it retroactive. Next week we shall probably be asked to vote him a salary as High Commissioner. And during all this time he has not had to go back to his electorate, as Winston Churchill in England, and the Minister of Inland Revenue in this country did only a short while ago. The whole thing is false from top to bottom. Any fair-minded man will admit that the whole thing is a mess, and contrary to constitutional practice in this country.
