speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
Oj>
the question of the need of establishing ' parliamentary under secretaryships I do not intend to offer any observations at the present time, but, in order that there may he no misapprehension in regard to the circumstances under which I assumed and occupy the office of Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence, I think it is right that I should make a statement to the House.
Every hon. member in this House knows
o.f the large numlber of cases throughout the country in which public-spirited citizens are willingly and gladly giving vountary service in connection with war work. Therefore, I think it is not surprising that a member of Parliament should wish to share in this public service.
I received in July last an intimation from my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) that further assistance was required in the Department of Militia and Defence. The correspondence disclosed the fact that the burden cast by the war upon all departments bad become increasingly onerous, and particularly so in the case of the Department of Militia and Defence. Perhaps I cannot do better than read the correspondence. It is as follows:
Ottawa, 9th July, 1916. Dear Mr. McCurdy:-
As you are aware, the burdens oast by the war on all departments having to do with its prosecution have become increasingly onerous.
In particular, the work of the Minister of Militia and Defence has become very great. The nature of his duties also constantly call him away from his department. To assist him, and to provide for continuity in the conduct of the department's business and business policy, the minister. Major General Sir Sam Hughes, has requested the Governor in Council through me to establish an office to he known as Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence, and to select a member of the House to perform the duties above referred to.
In connection with your offer to serve in any capacity, the Minister of Militia has, recognizing your business qualifications, experience, and attention to public duties, suggested your appointment, and I am pleased to say that my colleagues gladly concur in his nomination.
It is proposed that the Governor in Council shall forthwith establish the office referred to, and until Parliament has made provision, the appointment cannot carry any salary, allowance, or fees of any kind. The Government will he prepared, however, to recommend any reasonable request in that connection.
My colleagues and I realize the demands already made on your time in connection with

your parliamentary duties and appreciate that, if you accept this position of public service, necessarily you will be called upon to make further sacrifice in connection with your business affairs.
If, however, you can see your way clear to accede to their request, we shall he pleased to have your appointment completed at once.
Yours very truly,
R. L. Borden.
Mr. F. B. McCurdy, M.P.,
Halifax, N.S.
To which I replied on July 14, 1916.
July 14, 1916.
Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden,
President of the Privy Council,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir Robert:-
Replying to your favour of the 9th inst., I desire to record my appreciation of your attitude and that of your colleagues towards me. I am gratified that the Honourable the Minister of Militia himself should suggest me for the appointment referred to by you.
In connection with the prosecution of the war, I am still desirous of serving in any capacity for which I may be considered competent by the minister. It, therefore, affords me pleasure to concur in the suggestion made in your letter, and to say that if the appointment is made, the duties attaching to the post will have the best attention of which I am capable.
With regard, however, to remuneration, I desire to say that my acceptance is made conditional upon the understanding that I shall not receive in connection therewith any salary, fee, or allowance of any kind. I shall be only too pleased to place in this regard my services and whatever capacity and business experience I possess freely at the disposal of the State while the war lasts.
Yours faithfully,
F. B. McCurdy.
That was my feeling at the time, that is my feeling to-day, and I wish to make it cleaT that should Parliament in its discretion see fit to vote a salary for the Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence I have no intention myself of retaining that salary.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
That is the only
point of difference between your humble servant and my hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) I positively object to any person in the employ of this Government working for nothing, when there is a salary attached to the job. My good friend, I presume, is blessed with this world's goods. Many of us are not. Why should a man, of possibly as great ability as my hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne, be debarred by having the precedent set that he must not take office because there are young men, whose fathers had money, or who have money themselves, and who are willing to do the work for

nothing? I claim that when a man offers his services to the Government he is entitled to his pay, and that he should take it. It is all right to hand it over to the Red Cross or to any other fund if he likes. That is another matter. My hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne knows that I never could harmonize with him on that point. Let every man be paid a fair wage, and then if he chooses to hand it over to some worthy object, let him do so. I maintain that this business of giving jobs to gentlemen because they are in a position to do the work for nothing is wrong. You have no control of, or hold upon, them, and after all it is the question of responsibility for which we must have regard. If the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne will accept the salary of the office, and then hand the money back to the treasury, or to the Red Cross, he should do so and not establish a precedent whereby some other worthy member of Parliament equally as capable as himself, and equally entitled to get the job, is subjected to the contrast that for one office a salary is paid and for another there is no salary.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
It is perfectly apparent
from the statement of the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) that he is not disposed to accept any salary for his services. That declaration will be received by many of his friends in Nova Scotia with a great deal of gratification. But the hon. member for Victoria and Hali-burton (Sir Sam Hughes) says that it must be insisted upon that the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne shall accept his salary and dispose of it in whatever way he thinks proper. I think it would be well in the interests of the hon. member for Shelburne himself that the matter should be cleared up. If he is working for a salary, and if he is going to accept that salary, I think it would be well that the general public should know it. If he is going to work without any salary he should get the credit that his sacrifice entitles him to. There seems to be several gentlemen who are willing to give their services to this Government for nothing. The other evening, when we were discussing the appointment of Mr. Henderson as chairman of the committee to inquire into the operations of the William Davis Company, it was said that he was going to work for nothing. I am bound to say, quite apart from the case of the hon. member for
Queens and Shelburne, that I am extremely suspicious when gentlemen outside of this House offer their services to the country free of charge. I might enumerate several others who are offering their services, and I could only repeat what has been said by my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes). I think that this Government is in a position to fairly compensate any citizen for valuable services rendered. I do not think that it makes for confidence in the work of these gentlemen, or for the reputation of the Government that they should offer and give their services free of charge. Whenever services are accepted, there should be proper compensation for them.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I appreciate, as I am sure every member of this House appreciates, the motive behind the words of the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy), but I object, as one member of this House, and one of the citizens of this country who was not bom with a silver spoon in his mouth, to any such practice as the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne suggests.
If I have any criticism to offer in regard to the conduct of public business in this country it is that there seems to be rather too much a tendency for jobs to go to men who have any amount of money, men who are in the millionaire class. It is all right for a man who can count his money by the millions and who is patriotic enough to offer to perform certain duties which he can perform without drawing any salary. I have not a word to say against his motives; the motives of that gentleman are just as good and sound as mine would be in offering to perform those duties. But the amount of this world's goods that I possess would make it impossible for me to do what he is willing to do for nothing. Now, Mr. Chairman, it strikes me that in a country like Canada, which is, and I hope will always be, a democratic country,-notwithstanding that we seem to be piling up a number of knights and barons, rather more than I like to see-I say that it is subversive of democracy and against its best interests that men should be allowed to take offices, no matter how faithfully they perform the duties of those offices, and not accept reasonable pay for the work so performed. If you followed that out to its logical conclusion, you would encourage the general public to believe that that is the right thing to do and you would soon have a demand in this country that, in order to save a few thousand dollars here or there, we should appoint to these import-



ant positions only millionaires and people of that class, able to do the work without remuneration. I object to that most strongly. It seems to me that the creation of these three positions that have been mentioned here is a matter that should be considered by us on its merits. So far as the work of Sir George Perley is concerned, Sir George Perley is a wealthy man and has shown himself from 1911 up to the present to be a true and patriotic Canadian, willing, although a man of large business interests, to devote his time without remuneration to the service of his country. He is engaged in work over there, and what I said a few moments ago in regard to paying the under secretaries applies also to him. We as members of this House, should consider whether this position, overseas is necessary or is not necessary. I for one believe that the appointment of an Overseas Minister of Militia was a wise appointment to make and I believe further that, since we have appointed a gentleman to that position, he should be paid for the work he does in it.
We have also to consider, it seems to me, whether it was a wise thing to appoint the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) and the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark) to the positions they occupy. I am disposed, as is my friend who spoke a few minutes ago, to accept the statement of the Prime Minister that he has been greatly relieved by the work done by the hon. * member for Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark). These hon. gentlemen have been appointed to certain positions to do certain work. It is for us to consider whether those positions were necessary. If we consider or agree that those positions were necessary, then it is up to us to consider how much should be paid as remuneration for filling those positions.
I want to say to some hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House-who are mighty saving of dollars sometimes when those dollars are being expended from this side of the House, that they had better look over their own history. We have not the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) here to-day. If we had, I suppose he would be objecting on the ground of economy to the paying out of a few thousands of dollars to these under-secretaries. And yet in what position is that gentleman? He is in the position of having taken royalties and put them in his own pocket, royalties that belonged to the treasury of this country, and he has kept them there, and there has been no condemnation of that practice on his part by his leader or by any

other hon. gentleman opposite. That is a fact, there is no getting around it, a fact which he admitted himself on the floor of the House; that he took royalties on coal lands or mines in the West, that he has that money in his pocket at the present time-unless he returned it before 'starting for Winnipeg just lately-and I want to say to hon. gentlemen, when they are talking about economy and saving a few dollars here or there, that they should get after their own member, the member for Edmonton, and ask him to put back into the treasury the money which he took wrongfully, which he is not entitled to, and for taking which, any man who was not a member of this House would be criticised in language which I am not permitted to use.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
I am not surprised at the attitude taken by the hon. member for Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy). Anyone might have expected that from him. We all knovV that he is favoured with a large fortune, and so is Sir George Perley, who [DOT] is in the millionaire class. For me it is not a question of money, although I say that at the present moment it has not been demonstrated that these new offices are needed; more particularly I urge that we should not create new offices when we have to make the soTry admission that Canada to-day is borrowing at usurious rates of interest in New York, when we consider that the bonds of Canada are selling at 98, bearing 6 per cent interest. Surely it is time for Canadians to cry halt. When we are spending nearly one million dollars a day it is no time for the Government to create new offices, the necessity for which is not demonstrated.
But this is not the point which I raise this afternoon. It is not a question of [DOT]money; it is not a question of dollars and cents; there is a principle which is far above dollars and cents. I say that Sir George Perley, millionaire as he is, Overseas Minister as he has been created, receives emoluments from his office, and because of such emoluments should come back before the people of Canada and be re-elected, as all ministers of the Crown in Canada are re-elected. I was made Solicitor General a few years ago, a subordinate position in the Government. I had to seek reelection in the county of Gaspe. Two years afterwards I became a minister of the Crown, hut as I had been re-elected as Solicitor General it was not necessary for me to return before the people. But every new minister of the Crown must seek re-

election ait the hands of his electors. I want to know by what divine right should we be creating to-day that new family compact, because this departure is nothing else but a new edition of the old family compact. To-day it is Sir George Perley; tomorrow it will be Sir Joseph Flavelle; the day after to-morrow it will be Sir Clifford Sifton

all those millionaires will be given offices in the Government to save the country and to save the Empire without reelection. Canada is being dominated by a caste of war profiteers, by a coterie of millionaires and plutocrats.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
It is evident that the hon. *member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) had read the reports from the Winnipeg Convention before he addressed the Souse, because I cannot understand how otherwise the milk of human kindness would have become so curdled in the hon. gentleman's noble breast. I will not allude further to his extraordinary attack upon an hon. gentleman who is not here present in his seat to defend himself, but who, before those who know him best, evidently requires no defence.
I listened with real interest to what my hon. and genial friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) had to say. lie expressed himself as shocked at one charge which he seemed to find in the language my hon. friend from Rouville levelled against the Government. Observing that immediately in front of my hon. friend from, Peterborough the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) is sitting, and recalling that that hon. gentleman has made, not one charge but a whole series of meet dam,aging charges against the Government ever since he wrote his famous letters to the Prime Minister last fall, I cannot understand how the hon. gentleman from West Peterborough would be so shocked at one charge made by the hon. member for Rouville, and overlook completely all the charges made by the hon, member for Victoria.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: Who said I overlooked them?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: If he has not overlooked them, we have not heard any protest trcrn him.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext: That is another thing.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTION FOR THEIR APPOINTMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, that is quite another thing, and I am glad to find by the hon. gentleman's intimation that he has not overlooked them. We shall expect to hear from him on that subject. Up to the 267i
present, the Government completely overlooked them, and these charges remain, not only unrefuted, but uncontradicted in every particular.
I desire to refer to a question that my hon. friend from Victoria addressed to the Prime Minister, and which remains unanswered. He asked what kind of structure we should put up if one minister built one story and another minister built another story, and the hon. gentleman received no reply to that question. There is historic precedent for such an inquiry. That is precisely the same question as was addressed on a famous occasion by Hennessey to Dooley, the philosopher of Archey Road, with whom my hon. friend, the member for Victoria will be familiar. They were discussing the construction of the national edifice in the United States, and Hennessey asked Dooley what kind of building would be put up if he had one kind of man at one story and another kind of man at another story, and Dooley said, " The outer walls would resemble the homeward tracks from a wake." That is the answer to my hon. friend's question. The Prime Minister told us that he had received a letter from Sir George Perley stating that he did not intend to accept any salary as overseas Minister of Militia. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) stated a short time ago that he also hiad declined to accept any salary in the position which he has been filling for some time, and to which it is now proposed to appoint him by the resolution under consideration. In view of these two statements, I submit to the Prime Minister in all seriousness that neither of these salaries should be voted. What is the sense in voting salaries which gentlemen say they will not accept? On the other hand, if they are voted, the effect of voting them is to place these two hon. gentlemen under an unjust suspicion. Either those salaries should be dropped, or if voted, they should he accepted; and from that point of view I entirely agree with what has been said by my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwiards). I think the position he took with regard to these salaries, and with regard to the creation of similar positions with salaries attached, is entirely the correct and constitutional position to take.
That brings me to another matter which was briefly referred to by the Prime Minister, but which is of transcendent importance to the people of Canada. In criticising the objections offered by the leader of the Opposition to this resolution, the

Prime Minister drew an analogy between what is proposed under this resolution, in so far as the position of Minister of Militia Overseas is concerned, and what had been done by Mir. Lloyd George in creating an authority outside Parliament. In his reference	to that authority created	outside Parliament in Great Britain, I submit with great	respect,	the
Prime Minister was hardly correct. He said that, owing to the pressure of his war duties, Mr. Lloyd George had found it necessary to divest himself of certain duties as Prime Minister within Parliament, and to depute the performance of those duties to Mr. Bonar Law. That, I submit, is not exactly what occurred in Great Britain. Mr. Lloyd George, in conjunction with Lord Curzon and Lord Milner has, in the opinion of some of the best thinkers of Great Britain, taken away from Parliament a number of its constitutional privileges and liberties, and has set up outside Parliament an autocratic council or committee which, if it has any analogy at all, is analogous to the position of affairs in the United States, where the cabinet is not elected, but is selected, and where the President does not sit in the House, bu; only goes to the House on certain occasions and addresses that Chamber. I have read articles protesting against the denuding of Parliament in Great Britain, written by some of the best thinkers and most eminent men in England, and pointing out that while this condition of, affairs lasts Parliament is a mere registering body, and is not a legislative or administrative body in the sense that it was before this- autocratic council of four was created practically outside the jurisdiction of Parliament. So that, agreeing with that view of the functions and duties and responsibilities of this small council in Great Britain, I do not think the analogy which my right hon. friend sought to draw with reference to the present resolution was a very happy one, or, indeed, an appropriate one. As the leader rf the Opposition pointed out, this resolution is divided into three parts, one relating to the Minister of Militia Overseas, and the others to the two undersecretaries. I do not intend to criticise the creation of these offices further than I have already done, nor to refer to the gentlemen who, it is proposd, shall fill these offices; but I entirely agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Victoria and other hon. gentlemen, that the creation of this second Minister of Militia is entirely unnecessary. If there are duties to be performed overseas, they can be per-fMr. Murphy-1
formed by an official who would be responsible to the Minister of Militia here, who would have a seat in this House, and who would be responsible to Parliament. Already we have practically two Ministers of Justice. I cannot at the moment recall that that has operated to the public disadvantage, but it is an anomaly which did not present itself heretofore. Now, we have two Ministers of Militia. As the hon. gentleman from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) intimated, who can say but to-morrow we shall have two ministers of another department, and the day after two ministers of a third department, and so on? I think it is a dangerous innovation, and does not make for the benefit of representative institutions as we understand them in this country, and will not be approved by those who are apprehensive, and naturally apprehensive, regarding the gradual diminution of democratic government, not only in this country, buc in several of the Allied countries engaged in this war. My hon. friend from West Peterborough has criticised the salaries of the under secretaries and disapproved of them, but, curiously I thought with all respect to him, he said, he would shut his eyes and vote for the salary, because we were near an election. I submit to my hon. friend and to my other colleagues in this House on both sides that that is scarcely a good reason for supporting a resolution of this kind.

As far as the amount of the salary is concerned, that of the Overseas Minister is exactly in accordance with the salary which is fixed for ministers of the Crown. I do not desire to enter into a discussion as to the constitutional changes in Great Britain. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) that the House go into Committee of the Whole to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide:
1.	That His Majesty may acquire on such terms and conditions satisfactory to the Governor in Council as may be set out in the agreement to be made with the owners and pledgees of not less than five-sixths thereof.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
and for a price to be determined as hereinafter provided, the six hundred thousand shares of capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company (par value sixty million dollars), not now held by the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty.
2.	That the Governor in Council shall appoint one arbitrator, the said owners and pledgees shall appoint another, and the two so appointed shall appoint a third, or failing agreement as to such appointment, the third arbitrator shall be appointed by the senior judge of the Exchequer Court.
3.	The said arbitrators shall determine the value of the said six hundred thousand shares as of the date of the said agreement and the :said arbitrators shall proceed in a summary way and may apply their own judgment in -determining such value and may receive with respect thereto, such reports and statements [DOT]authenticated in such way as they may decide *and such evidence as they may deem necessary or helpful, examine witnesses under oath and hear the parties by counsel or representatives and that the unanimous determination of the arbitrators shall be final, but should the determination not be unanimous an appeal from such determination shall lie to the Supreme Court of Canada on behalf of the Governor in Council, or if the owners or pledgees, upon any question of law or fact, such appeal to be made within thirty days from the rendering of the determination.
4.	That the amount of the value so determined shall be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, or otherwise secured in accordance with the terms of the said agreement.
5.	That upon the making of said agreement, at least five-sixths of the said six hundred thousand shares shall be transferred to the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty, and if there be any of said six hundred thousand shares not transferred as aforesaid, the Governor in Council may declare said shares to be the property of the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty, and the same shall thereupon become the property of His Majesty and shall be paid for pro rata with the shares so transferred.
6.	That so soon as said five-sixths of said shares has been transferred as aforesaid, the Governor in Council may assist the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or any company included in the Canadian Northern Railway system, in paying and settling any indebtedness of such company or postponing the payment thereof on such terms as may be agreed upon, and for such purposes may make advances out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, may guarantee payment in whole or in part, and may give the obligation or securities of the Government in connection therewith.
7.	That the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and each company included in the Canadian Northern Railway system, shall from time to time do such acts and things, make and issue such agreements, obligations and securities in connection with the payment or settlement or postponement of payment of the said claims as the Minister of Finance may require.
8.	That the necessary qualification shares for directors may be transferred to or allowed to remain in their names by the Minister of Finance on such conditions as he may determine.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a very important resolution, important for our whole country and especially so for the western part of the Dominion. It will be observed that there is a very slight attendance in the Chamber. I do not see on this side of the House, nor at the moment on the other side of the House, more than one hon. member from west of lake Superior. The hon. members who represent that section of the country are, at the present time, engaged in a very important meeting elsewhere. Would it not be preferable, instead of going into Committee of the Whole, to refer this resolution to a small special committee to secure information which we must thresh out in Committee of the Whole? So far as the financial position of the company is concerned, we have only a statement entitled "Financial statements respecting the Canadian Northern Railway company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company." We have no information whether this is the whole of the liability of the Canadian Northern Railway company or whether there are other liabilities. I understand there are other liabilities beyond those mentioned in that statement, being balances due by the company to contractors and so forth. We have no statement at all as to the actual condition of the road, how much is needed for immediate expenses, what are the prospects of the company, or what was the business transacted last year, except in a very general way. If the resolution were referred to a small special committee, the general manager could be summoned, and a good deal of information acquired which it would otherwise be difficult to obtain. I make that suggestion to my hon. friend in the hope that it may be favourably considered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

I would suggest to my right hon. friend that we might go into committee on the resolution and perhaps pass it, and then, before the second reading takes place, we could consider my right hon. friend's suggestion. It is desirable, of course, that all information that is relevant should be afforded, but whatever discussion could take place upon the resolution could also take place in committee after the second reading of the Bill. There is no difficulty either in the one case or in the other. Perhaps we had better go into committee on the resolution. discuss the resolution, and perhaps, if there is no objection, pass it

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I am afraid that would be quite impracticable. The securities of the companies are bonds and debenture stock, which have been issued largely in Great Britain. It would be quite impossible to ascertain the bondholders, because they must be thousands in number The securities pass from hand to hand, and an owner to-day might not be an owner to-morrow. The Canadian Northern made some short term loans in New York, and the same remark would apply to those. I think there is full information in the printed document as to the financial position of the company. The securities outstanding, the amount of the floating loan and other liabilities, are all shown in the statement certified by the auditors of the company. If there is any other special information that would seem necessary in order that the committee might come to a determination upon the matter, we should, of course, endeavour to obtain it. I do not see what bearing the matter of the owners of the securities has upon the question. The transaction, although one of magnitude, is in reality a very simple one, namely, to acquire the outstanding stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company which controls all the underlying companies. We have pretty full information as to all matters relevant to a consideration of the resolution.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
This question is of such vital importance to the people of Canada, particularly at the present time, that it is wise that we should make progress slowly and be sure of every step. It is important, not only from the standpoint of the liabilities to be assumed, but on account of the departure being made in removing from private to public ownership one of the great transcontinental highways of the country and its various branches and subsidiary companies.
The policy of public ownership is one that has been tried in many countries of the world, including our own, .and the principle itself, as well as the details of this proposition, ought to be viewed from all aspects. As I said the other day, I am not so sure that a government monopoly would be ia very great improvement upon a private monopoly, so far as the real details of operation .and the benefits .to ibe derived by the public are concerned. Railway managers the world over, like the managers of every other concern, .are naturally most .anxious to have .a good showing for their enterprises, and once the incentive to service, which is brought about by competition, is removed it is not so sure that a monopoly, even if it be a public monopoly, would be the best thing for the public. In this case, however, the question of a monopoly does not arise to any great extent, as two of the great railway systems of Canada are not included.
The Government has decided to embark upon a policy of public ownership of the Canadian Northern system. Friends of that .policy-and there are many throughout Canada-want to be .assured that public ownership is not being burdened with such a colossal financial load at the outset as to hamper materially the .success cf the undertaking. We ought to view fairly, I think, the amount of money .that has been expended upon the Canadian Northern railway system, and its present value as well, .and then ask ourselves the question: Could the Government construct this system for the amount presented to us as the fbture liability of the country on account of taking over the Canadian Northern? If we pay altogether too much for the property .some person may arise in a few years and blame government ownership for a failure, which, might not be the fault of government ownership at all, but the fault of an improvident bargain. I am not saying that such is the case, but am pointing out that in making this departure the members of the House ought to make sure, so far .as possible, that the Government is getting full value for the liability which it proposes to assume, or the project cannot be the success it might otherwise be.
The fixed charges have a great deal to do with the success or failure of any business enterprise. If the fixed charges be altogether too high, then, although the enterprise may be a fairly good, paying concern, it is hampered to the extent of these excess fixed charges. .
In this connection let me point out that there are three ways in which the Canadian Northern could become the property of the country. First, by allowing it to go

into a receiver's hands, and the Government becoming the owners of the system by process of law. It is true, as I view it, that in that case the Government as purchaser would perhaps have as its competitors other interests that might desire this line and would be willing to pay a fairly good price for it. But, on the other hand, if a private corporation were prepared to pay a certain amount for this system it would be fairly good evidence that the road was worth that amount, because a private concern would not be willing to pay a sum on which it could not realize a fair return. As I said the other day, personally I am rather disinclined to favour the idea of a receivership for the reasons which I then gave, and which I think will be obvious to all the members of the House. The Dominion and the provinces have guaranteed a large amount of the securities of this system. Having guaranteed those securities, it has struck me that if the project which the Government has backed with these guarantees were allowed to go into a receiver's hands, it might be injurious to our financing in the markets of the world as a government, because as a parliament we have practically endorsed the notes of this concern. Speaking for myself, I do not view the idea of allowing the road to go into the hands of a receiver in the same light in which such a proceeding might be viewed if financial conditions in Canada at the present time were not strained on account of the great burdens we have assumed and must assume by reason of the war.
Another method of taking over the road would be by expropriation, just as the Government can acquire any other property, and allowing the Exchequer Court to decide the value. That method is debatable, and I will not deal with it.
The other method is the one proposed by the Government, that the Government should become the possessor of the common stock of the enterprise, and thus really become the owner of the system. In doing that, if the company be allowed to retain its entity and idenity as a corporation, the Canadian Northern railway, with the Government the owner of the stock, would be liable for all the bonds, guaranteed and unguaranteed, and other liabilities as well. While at present the Government is liable for the securities which it has guaranteed, when it becomes the owner of the property it will have to assume liability for all the securities that have not

been guaranteed, as well as the floating liabilities.
Let us see what we are assuming, for I take it that before we proceed far with this Bill we must know what our entire liabilities will be when we become the owner of all this stock. The statement placed before us does not, I submit, give us all the information required. The Finance Minister will remember that when aid was last given to the Canadian Northern, it was agreed that there should be a continuous audit, the Government being part owner of the system. This report contains an audit, but it has only been brought down to June 30, 1916, over a year ago. In order to know exactly what the conditions are, the House ought to be possessed of a certified audit of the Canadian Northern accounts up to June 30, 1917, with any additional information that could be given for the period intervening between June 30, 1917, and the present date.
As to the value, it would not be amiss if I were to call the attention of the committee to a portion of the majority report of the Royal Commission, the gentlemen assenting to this report being Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth. On page XII of that report I find reference to the Canadian Northern Railway system which bears on the point to which I have been directing my observations:
Value of Canadian Northern Undertaking.
1.	Cash Investment.
The property investment of the Canadian Northern Railway system is stated in the balance sheet of June 30, 1916, at $494,112,489.34. This figure admittedly has been written up to include $100,000,000 of capital stock. And this stock, as we have already said, was issued without any cash consideration. We have endeavoured to ascertain the actual cost of the system. From the company's official reports and special statements supplied to us, we have ascertained that the maximum cash investment that can have been made in the property is $383,302,451.33.
That is the statement. Then follow tables which I need not give to the Committee. After making some calculations, including the amount of stock held in subsidiary companies, not held by the Canadian Northern, the Drayton-Acworth Report concludes :
We find then $370,000,000 to be the maximum possible cost of the Canadian Northern system as at present existing. In other words, as indeed is frankly admitted by Canadian Northern witnesses, the Canadian Northern shares represent no cash investment.
If the House will bear with me I want read one or two other paragraphs. There

is another one dealing with the physical basis. The report proceeds.
2.	Physical Basis.
But money cost is hot all. We decided also to ascertain the approximate value, on the basis of reproduction cost, of the property as it exists to-day. And we rely on Professor Swain's valuation for this purpose. This valuation is, in his opinion, a liberal estimate of the fair cost of reproducing new, at prewar prices of labour and material, the system at present existing. It includes property belonging to the system at its estimated cost, if it had to be acquired or constructed to-day. And therefore it not only gives the company credit for lands which it in fact owns, even though it obtained them as a grant; but it also credits the company with the increment of land values since the date of the original acquisition. And these two items are quite large.
It will be noted that in making this statement the Royal Commission is endeavouring to get at what it would cost to reproduce the Canadian Northern Railway system at the prices and values ranging just before the war, as it would not be fair to take the scale of wages and prices of everything at the present time, because after the war is over these will drop again. In making its valuation it gives the system credit for the land values, and the increase of these land values since they were acquired by the Canadian Northern Railway company .from the Parliament of Canada. Then it proceeds:
Professor Swain's method of arriving at his results are fully explained in his report, which is printed as an appendix hereto. He makes the total cost of reproduction new, $397,441,567. Prom this he deducts for depreciation $40,031,889, making the cost of reproduction of the property in its present condition $357,409,678. This, however, does not include equipment. The equipment was inspected by Mr. Buchanan and, on the basis of his report as to quantities and condition, a valuation has been made by Mr. W. H. Chadbourn, C.E., chief engineer of our valuation staff. He finds the cost of reproduction new at pre-war prices to be $56,590,418, and the depreciation to be $11,250,433, making the present value $45,339,985. Putting the two valuations together, we have $402,749,663 as the fair cost of reproducing the entire physical Canadian Northern system in Its present condition. Now the outstanding liabilities (bonds, debentures, notes, and bank and other loans) of the company, exceed $400,000,000.
Reckoning on this basis, it appears that the liabilities are practically equal to the reproduction cost of the physical property. But the physical property does not all belong to the Canadian Northern shareholders. There are minority holdings in several of the subsidiary undertakings. And the Canadian Northern interest in these undertakings only corresponds to its percentage proportion of their respective share capitals. This implies a reduction of more than $10,000,000 in the estimate of the
assets belonging to the Canadian Northern, shareholders.
We find then that, on the physical basis, the value of the property of the Canadian Northern shareholders is distinctly less than the amount of the liabilities against it. Oru this basis the equity of the shareholders must be regarded as non-existent.
Now I propose to read a paragraph referring to the Canadian Northern as a going concern. It is as follows:
3.	Going Concern.
A third basis of estimate is the value of the property for sale as a going concern. A purchaser would not consider either original cost or reproduction cost as of much importance. The price he would pay would be based on earning power, present and potential. On this basis he would consider how far the Canadian Northern is at present short of covering its fixed charges, how long it will take to reach equilibrium, how much new capital. will have to be spent, how soon a dividend may be expected and at what rate. Calculating on this basis, in the light of the figures set out above, it is evident that no purchaser would offer for the property a sum amounting to the total of its liabilities.
The commissioners conclude in these words:
Conclusion As to Canadian Northern.
We conclude, therefore, that the shareholders of the company have no equity either on the ground of cash put in, or on the ground of physical reproduction cost, or on the ground of the saleable value of their property as a going concern.
If then the people of Canada have already found or assumed responsibility for the bulk of the capital; if they must needs find what further capital is required; and if they must make up for some years to come considerable deficits in net earnings, it seems logically to follow that the people of Canada should assume control of the property. We return later to the Canadian Northern Company in order to set out our recommendations as to its ownership and management in the future and as to the returns to be offered to the existing shareholders.
'T"have read that to give the committee the viewpoint of the Royal Commission, on the value of the property, and the intrinsic value of the physical assets of the company as well as the lack of value of the shares. They say that the shareholders have no equity, or that the equity is not worth anything.
Let me take up the figures as set out in the financial statement of the Canadian Northern system, audited, as I pointed out to the minister, only to June 30, 1916.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The company's financial year ends on June 30. If, with the information we have, the minister could give us the net earnings or the gross earnings and the expenditure, and the liabilities, if any, incurred during the year, it would perhaps answer the purpose.
I find that in the statement laid on the Table of the finances of the company up to June 30, 1916, the company, as stated by the Royal Commission, (placed their property investment, including their equipment, acquired securities, etc., at $494,112,489.34. Taking the whole statement, I find that they place their assets at $578,747,291.25 and the liabilities, which include a surplus on land account and railway account of about $40,000,000, at the same amount.
But let me take up just for a moment the securities guaranteed by the Federal and Provincial Governments. I find on page 5 of this report that the Dominion and Provincial Governments have guaranteed bonds, debenture stock, to the extent of $104,613,247.83.
The bonds guaranteed by the provinces are as follows:

In addition to this list of securities guaranteed by federal or provincial authorities, we find, on pages 6 and 7, that there are unguaranteed securities to the extent of $147,803,745.54, or a total of $359,931,635.64. In addition to these amounts it must 'be remembered that nearly all these lines were subsidized over and above the guarantees given, so that what we have now guaranteed together with the provinces and what we have given in subsidies constitutes a [Sir Thomas White.}
very large portion of the money that has gone into the Canadian Northern system. I havie gone over this hurriedly, just to draw attention to two or three points; first, we ought to know absolutely what all our liabilities will be when we take possession of this system-all tthe liabilities. I have outlined the guaranteed securities. Then I think it will be admitted that, in addition to our own guaranteed securities of $104,000,000, we will eventually have to see that the provinces are protected in their $107,000,000 guaranteed bonds1 as the property becomes ours, and, in addition, we will have to assume liability for $147,000,000 unguaranteed securities. But, in addition to this, there is a large floating indebtedness. I am of the opinion that, in addition to any amount included in this statement, it will be found that there are various bills payable throughout the Dominion to contractors and others, which the Government will have to assume if they become owners of this system.
Before very much progress is made we ought to have before us the amount of these other liabilities. Instances have been called to my attention, contractors have visited me, to see if the Government was likely to take over this line, and what I knew about it. And they asked, if the road were taken over would they be sure of having their bills settled. The Government could take the position, it is true, with regard to these outstanding accounts, that the liability was that of the Maokenzie-Mann company, and that when we take over the property we will not assume the liability. Legally, I suppose they could take that position. But the Government would not argue-and the people would not allow it to argue, and Parliament would not consent to the proposition that the country should take over, say, a bridge for which the contractors had not been paid, and leave that account unpaid. If the contractors can substantiate their accounts, I take it for granted the Government will have to assume liability in respect for them.
Then there is another matter to which the Drayton report refers, for which I am not going to take their figures, but will just make a general statement, because I have not had time to go into it. There are many enterprises in which the Canadian Northern is engaged at the present time. There are the terminals at Montreal, the Vancouver terminals, betterments all along the line, improvements yet to be finished in the city of Quebec, some probably in the

city of Toronto-in fact, in <a great many towns, the Canadian Northern is making betterments, as well as along their line. We ought to have a statement before we proceed to purchase this property, not only as to the value of the line itself and as to the liabilities, but as to how much money it will take to complete the undertakings which the system has launched; because, without the completion of these undertakings the system will not at all be perfect according to the view of the present proprietors and managers. In addition to that,
I think it is fair to assume that millions of dollars will be needed for betterments along the line of the Canadian Northern-the	strengthening of bridges, the
improvement, not of grades, but in ballasting and improvements in a great many ways which the Finance Minister understands, and which the Minister of Railways understands perhaps better. That will take millions of dollars. Then, it is admitted on all sides that the Canadian Northern, like all other railways, is short of rolling stock. The Canadian Pacific railway is equipped with, I think, seven freight cars to the mile, while the Canadian Northern has three. The fair proportion at least for the Canadian Northern business would be five freight cars to the mile. This will cost millions of dollars, too. Roughly speaking we are entering upon a scheme of purchase, the value of which we do not know, with a liability for completion the figures for which we ought to have in our hands, with a further liability for betterment the amount of which we ought to know, and with a still further necessary liability for rolling stock and motive power. These things we must know before we can tell just how far we are going, or what investment we intend to make in this great project of public ownership. Another point that comes to my mind is that in some portions of the main line, and particularly in the subsidiary companies, the securities have been disposed of at a very small rate. Their face value is par. The moment the Government becomes the owner of this road, unless legislation be introduced to prevent it, the value of these securities is likely to approximate par, perhaps not go to par, but it will be enhanced in value very materially, and this will open the door for an immense stock-jobbing process, out of which 'those who are sufficiently fortunate to be on the inside will be able to make fortunes compared with which anything gotten out of the Canadian Northern will be a bagatelle. During the past five years, if any
of the investors in the unguaranteed securities had been assured that they would receive the principal invested in these securities, with the interest up to date, they would have been happy individuals. I think it is feasible, when the Government is proposing to take over this property and become responsible for all these securities, to take steps to provide against the country becoming liable for par value for securities, the proceeds of which, in some instances, have been very much below par value. If on the other hand, no steps of that kind be taken, and these bonds become enhanced in value as they will, and the Government be obliged eventually to pay par, then we shall be compelled to pay millions upon millions of money for this road for which there is no value in the road itself, because no one pretends that par value has gone into the construction of the road. Just what that would amount to I am not prepared to say, but the Finance Minister would have an idea, if he has access to these securities-and they are all quoted to-day, I think. The question of the valuation of the shares is one that is very important. No one can accuse me of endeavouring to deal unfairly with any men of enterprise who have put their labour and money into these public concerns, but at the present time I am rather inclined to think that whatever might be given to Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann or the holders of the common stock of the Canadian Northern would be in the way of a recognition of the work they had performed in the development of Canada, rather than of any value as attached to the shares of the company. The Drayton-Acworth report comes out very strongly as to the lack of value in these shares. I am not going to discuss that, but in view of the fact that this system could now be taken possession of by the Government, either by allowing it to go into the hands of a receiver or by expropriation and a valuation placed upon it by the Exchequer Court, I am inclined to think that the value to be placed upon these 600,000 shares should not be made by a board of arbitrators at all.
But if the Government believe that something ought to be given, to Mackenzie and Mann on account of other considerations, the amount proposed to be given ought to be stated in the legislation; then we shall see whether or not Parliament will accept the proposal. I have not the most implicit confidence In what might be done by a board of arbitrators. If I had to leave a matter of this kind to any body at all, I

would rather leave it to the Exchequer Court, the hody that ought to deal with such things. Under present conditions, therefore, I aan rather inclined to think that if any method is to be adopted of placing a value on these shares, it should not be that of arbitration; the matter should be sent to the Exchequer Court. If the Royal Commission be right and the shareholders have no equity of any value, we ought to say so distinctly, rather than imply toy referring the matter to any body that the contrary is the case. On the other hand, if the Government see fit to recommend that an amount be given to the proprietors of the Canadian Northern Railway system in recognition of the development of the country through their work and in consideration of the Government's taking over their handiwork, I would suggest that the Government make up their mind what the amount is to be and, as I have said, have the amount stated in the legislation brought before the House. In any case, we ought to know what this enterprise i-s going to cost us before we go into it. Even if we have before us all the information in regard to the other items, a board of arbitrators might place upon these shares a valuation that would not be approved by the Exchequer Court. The country will not know what we are going to pay for this enterprise unless we state in definite terms what we propose to spend, if anything, for these shares. Full information should be brought down in reference to the proposed cost for betterments, for completion, for liability to contractors, so that we shall know just what we are assuming. I suggest that the Government abandon the idea of leaving to arbitration the valuation of these shares; that they Tattler make a concrete proposal so that we shall know what we are doing.
When aid was granted on a previous occasion to the Canadian Northern Railway system, there was a trust deed under which these securities were dealt with, carrying with it certain obligations on behalf of the company. I think it was called the new trust deed; its terms, are not to be found in the statute. In order that we may be informed whether the company have complied with the obligations embraced in that trust deed, it is fair that a copy of it should be placed before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has covered a good deal of ground and has asked for considerable information, much of which, I think, is already before the committee. I will take up his arguments 
as he proceeded. I think he fully outlined the three courses that are open to us in respect of this railway system. The first was that the Government might allow the Canadian Northern railway system to go into the hands of a receiver. It has been common ground on both sides of this House, *and it was the opinion of all the members of the Royal Commission appointed last year to deal with the problem of railways and transportation, that the Canadian Northern system and the Grand Trunk Pacific system' should not be allowed to go into the hands of a receiver. That was the position taken on both sides of the House- there may have been some exceptions-in 1914. For example, we find the right hon. leader of the Opposition in 1914-Hansard, page 3681-making the following statement:
I said a moment ago, and I repeat, that this enterprise must go on. It has heen conceived for the benefit of the Canadian people. We require this railway. My right hon. friend said he would not let it go into liquidation. It must not go into liquidation.
So that my hon. friend, in expressing the view that ;he did against allowing the Canadian Northern railway system to go into liquidation, merely agreed in the views which have been expressed on both sides of the House and by the members of the Royal Commission. My hon. friend adverted to a further consideration in that connection-the guarantees by the provinces and by the Dominion 9 p.m. Government. I stated when giving notice of these resolutions that the credit of the Dominion Government and of nearly all the provincial Governments of Canada, especially of the western provinces, .are inextricably involved with the credit of this great railway enterprise. That is an additional reason why the system should not be allowed to go into the hands of a receiver.
My hon. friend next mentioned the alternative of taking proceedings of expropriation and acquiring physical possession of the Canadian Northern Railway system. But one good reason why that should not be done is that the corporate entities of the several corporations embraced in the Canadian Northern Railway system would then be lost. The Dominion Government would then own the physical properties of the Canadian Northern Railway system just as it to-day owns the physical property of the Intercolonial and of the National Transcontinental from Moncton to Winnipeg. Upon these two latter railways there are no obligations. If the Government foreclosed and

took possession of all the physical properties of the system it would find itself in immediate ownership and also in immediate privity of obligation. Undoubtedly as a result there might be a great deal of litigation, because the Government's foreclosing under the $45,000,000 mortgage, or under the mortgage which was taken last year, would constitute default under most of the trust mortgages securing the underlying issues, with the result that receivers and liquidators might be appointed. I do not say that that result would necessarily follow, because if the Government foreclosed the holders of these securities would probably assume thaJt the Government would take care of the whole situation; oon-sequentiy they would not resort to litigation. Bat there seems no doubt as to their legal right to do so, and there might be a considerable amount of litigation. But that is not the main consideration why the Government should not foreclose and take over the physical properties in this system, although it is a very strong Teason for our not doing so.
The chief advantage of preserving the corporate identity of all the companies embraced in the system is that it maintains the financing which is already being done and it facilitates future financing; that^ is to say, by acquiring-and that is the third alternative, of which my hon. friend spoke -the entire $100,000,000 of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Bailway company, which in turn controls the stock of all the underlying companies, the Government is enabled to asist the corporate financing of that system. In other words, the system of finance which has been adopted and which is now being employed will continue to be employed, the Government giving such assistance as may, from time to time, be necessary.	_	_
My hon. friend spoke of the liabilities which the Dominion Government would assume in acquiring the stock of this road. Legally, the Government does not immediately become in privity with the holders of the outstanding securities and indebtedness on the road, but I should not be frank with the committee if I did not say that a Government taking over the capital stock and controlling an enterprise such as this would, of course, have the intention of continuing the system as a going concern. I might, however, point out that by acquiring the stock, we are in no materially different position from that in which we are to-day by reason of the guarantees which the Dominion has given in the past. The
$45,000,000 guarantee given in 1914 and the advance of $16,000,000 which we made last year are both secured by mortgages which come next after the mortgages securing the underlying bonds, debenture stock and other issues. The Government is, therefore, in this position, that, having regard to the guarantees given in the past-that is to say, the first mortgage guarantees and the guarantees given in 1914 and 1916 -unless we decide to forego the value of the equity which we hold under those mortgages, we practically must pay the interest on the underlying securities. That is also a very strong reason against a receivership, because if a receivership of the Canadian Northern Railway system took place, the Dominion Government and several of the provincial Governments would really be the receivers, because, being guarantors of the securities, they are liable. That is a very strong argument, as I think my hon. friend intimated, against placing these roads in liquidation.
I stated that most of the information for which my hon. friend asked was before the committee, and in order that we may see what we have and in order then that we may learn what further information is required, and that we may obtain it, I would like to refer to the information we have which was placed upon the Table the other day.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I heard what the minister said the other day.
'Sir THOMAS WHITE: The reason why the Canadian Northern requires aid at the present time is found conclusively in the financial statements which I have mentioned.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

The Government, instead olf bringing in a Bill to .afford aid as they did last year, have taken the ground that they will acquire the stock interests of the Canadian Northern owners, so that such aid as they afford will be aid to an enterprise which will be owned by the people o,f Canada instead of by the present proprietors.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

speechtext:
The Canadian
Northern officials presented their financial statement to the Government. They have certain .short-term liabilities maturing during the present year, which they^ may be [DOT]able to Tenew-probably will be able to renew.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Are they not all secured by Government guaranteed bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Nearly all of
them are. I believe they will be able to renew most of them, it not all. It must be borne in mind that we are in war time, and that it is not possible to speak with certainty as to whether loans secured, as my hon. friend has said, by the highest kind of collateral, can be renewed, although I believe myself that they will be renewed. But apart from that, by reason of the fact that the Canadian Northern has to take its net earnings to provide for betterments, for principal payments on rolling stock already required, and for new rolling stock, it is not possible for them to pay the interest on their underlying securities. Apart from the question of the renewal of short-term obligations, and the question of liability upon open account, which I believe is considerable, the Canadian Northern would require in the neighbourhood of $20,000,000 to pay interest obligations incurred and to be incurred in respect of securities taking priority over the $45,000,000 mortgage of the Dominion Government.
That was the position brought to our attention, and that being the position, instead of bringing down a Bill to give .aid to the extent of $20,000,000 or $25,000,000, which would, I think, be the minimum that would be required for the purpose of enabling the Canadian Northern to continue during the coming year as a solvent, going concern, the Government determined to take over the road for the people of Canada, so that any aid we might be called upon to furnish would inure to the benefit of the people of Canada.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would the minister state what is the amount of these short-term notes, where they are held-I presume either in London or New York, or both- and what are the guaranteed securities which have been hypothecated as security for these short-term notes?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

That is the point to which I was about to advert. I think my hon. friend will find all that information in the document which has been laid
on the Table. I want to find out just what we have before the House, because a great deal of the information asked for by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has already been placed on the Table; and when we have ascertained definitely what there is before the House, we can see what further information may reasonably be required, and endeavour to obtain it for the information of the members of the committee. My hon. friend fiom South Renfrew referred to the securities some of which he thought had been issued at a rate very much below par. That is not my understanding of the situation.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend answer my question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I intended first to deal with the long-date securities, and then come to the short-term securities, as I thought I could cover the ground better in that way. As I was saying, I am not aware that the securities of the Canadian Northern system have been sold at a heavy discount. On the contrary, in 1914, when a complete statement was made to this House as to the securities which had been issued and as to the amount which they had realized, the entire House was surprised that they had been so successful in placing at low interest Tates their securities by successive issues in London.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Some of the subsidiary

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: They did not issue the securities of the subsidiary companies. What they did was this:	The parent company would take the debenture stock or other securities of the subsidiary company, and against that issue their own debenture stock, and that debenture stock was issued at a very low rate of interest indeed1, even at that time, but exceedingly low as compared with the rates prevailing now.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That does not apply to the $147,000,000 of their securities against which there ie no debenture stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am speaking of the securities, and in passing, I want to make this observation. If ever there was a proper time to- acquire a railway system whose securities have been put out at a comparatively low rate of interest this is the time, because this is the time of high interest rates, and it will be many years indeed before it will be possible even for the Government of Canada to issue securities on the basis on which these securities

were issued by the Canadian Northern. The same argument -applies to the Grand Trunk. It is surprising at what a low rate of interest they put out their securities in view of the rates which prevail 'to-day for securities of the Imperial Government in -London, and of the 'Dominion Government here.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: This is a time when the Government is paying a very high rate of interest-an. -abnormal rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Are the figures given under "obligations" current liabilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I am glad that my hon. friend has mentioned tfiat. He has in mind, no doubt, what my hon. friend from South Renfrew said as to whether there was any indebtedness to contractors. I made careful inquiry about that, and I am getting a statement respecting it for the information of the committee. But I am told that all obligations to contractors are practically cleaned up. The secretary of the Railway Department tells me .that there is not on record with the department at the present time $100,000 of claims against the Canadian Northern Railway system. The situation has been cleared up since 1914 when there were large amounts outstanding due to contractors. There may be some outstanding liabilities, but if there are they are comparatively small.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
