subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
On the question of shortterm notes, would the minister give the committee some information? From the statement on page 12 it would appear that the amount borrowed in New York is $21,750,000. As collateral for that, there are $30,648,247.33 of Government securities.
Those would be guaranteed securities and there would be a margin of nearly nine millions. Is it open to the Canadian Northern Railway company to dispose of those guaranteed bonds that are now simply up as collateral? Is there anything in their agreement with the Government which would prevent them from selling them outright?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: There is no arrangement. If, when these notes matured- and it could not be done before-the Canadian Northern paid them off, the collateral would go to the Canadian Northern and would become part of the assets of that company.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: On the New York loans there is a margin of 50 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Not of real value; that is of face value. I have shown the committee that we have a complete statement as to Government guaranteed loans and as to unguaranteed funded debt; also a complete statement as to the short-term loans and current liabilities, and also a complete statement as to the collateral held as security for the latter. I have said that there is practically no indebtedness, outstanding to contractors.
I come now to the last point made by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), as to the mode of acquiring these shares, and also as to what would be the prospective requirements of this road for the next two years. The amount of money which may be spent upon any road is variable. There is no doubt that very Large sums might be spent upon the Canadian Northern to equip it properly in order that it may render the maximum of public service. On the other hand, -a road can be operated so as to give a reasonable public service with an expenditure that falls short of the amount which would be required to give an ideal service. Therefore, the amount which would be required upon the Canadian Northern for the next five years is a matter, necessarily, of estimate, and, not only that, but it is one which may depend upon the amount of money available. In the report which is before the House, made by Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Ac-worth, the matter is gone into very fully. There is an immense amount of information in this report. Nearly all the information asked for by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) will be found in it. On page XU there is a paragraph headed " Prospective Requirements of Canadian Northern." They siay:
The Canadian Northern estimate submitted
to us further calculated that, in course of the



next five years, the company will need to spend $12,500,000 of new capital for additions and betterments, and $25,000,000 for new equipment. We consider these estimates entirely inadequate, and especially so in relation to the estimate of 90 per cent increase in gross receipts. The company has acknowledge that its equipment is inadequate to take care of its existing business. That equipment stands in the company's books at $59,000,000. If the business were to increase 90 per cent, it would seem to need not $25,000,000 but over $50,000, 000 spent on new equipment to handle it.
That is to say, it $50,000,000 is spent the business will increase 90 per cent, and, of course, if .the business increased 90 per cent the expenditure would be .more than justified and to .a considerable extent liquidated by the earnings. The .amount that will be spent upon the Canadian Northern in the future is not susceptible of .accurate estimate, but if the Dominion Government is acquiring, as it is, .a system isnch as this, it should be its object, consistently with the financial position from time to time, to so improve the facilities' of the road as to render the best service to the public. The railway companies of Canada, with the exception of the Canadian Pacific, are all short of rolling stock. The fact that the Government of Canada will have to expend a certain .amount on the Canadian Northern line and large amounts for rolling stock for the road is, of course, no argument against the acquisition of that system, because the rolling stock is required to carry our agricultural .products to the seaboard .and to render .service generally to the commercial community. I do not know of any greater need in this country than that of rolling stock. The shops are working to their utmost1 capacity. The Minister of Railways is, I believe, willing to place orders for rolling stock practically .to the maximum of the capacity of the industrial establishments of the Dominion, to the end that the railways of Canada, the Intercolonial, the National Transcontinental, the Canadian Northern, may he equipped to render the best service to the public.
The bon. member for South Renfrew spoke of having a valuation made by the Exchequer Court. I .may say that in reaching .a determination to have the value of these shares fixed by an arbitration we were influenced by several considerations. I shall mention only two main considerations.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Why not give ns all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The two principal considerations. The Drayton-Acworth report recognizes that there should he equit-

able consideration for the owners of the stock of t.'ie Canadian Northern railway, and they suggest, in a plan which they propose, that arbitrators should determine the amount of stock which the Canadian Northern Railway owners and pledgees should be allowed to retain, and further the amount of the earnings of the Dominion Railway company which would be properly attributable to these shares. They recommend arbitration, and the mode which we have adopted in the resolution is precisely on all-fours with the recommendation of the Drayton-Acworth report; that is to say, that the owners of the stock should name one arbitrator, the Dominion Government should name another, and the two so appointed should name a third, or if they cannot agree that the third should be named by the senior judge of the Exchequer Court. There is another principal consideration. A legal controversy as to values, based upon all the factors that might enter into it, of a great railway system could extend quite conceivably over a year and a half or two years. I refer to the various factors entering into the valuation of the shares of a railway. They are all indicated by Professor Swain and are set out in the Drayton-Acworth report. In the first place, there is the question of physical value. I need not say to this House that if we had as able a lawyer on our side as the hon. gentleman from St. John, and the owners and pledgees had on the other side as equally able a lawyer, if he could be found in, Canada-

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: And both sides interested in making a strong case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: and both sides interested in making as strong a case as possible as to the value of the physical properties of a railway system of 9,500 miles, my hon. friend can see the vista opened to the legal imagination, as to the element of original value and all interest upon that, and the reproduction value. All that would be talked about by the lawyers, and all that would be dealt with by the expert witnesses who would be called by legion.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Marvellous possibilities in arbitrations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No, before the court.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I have been on arbitrations. Give me an arbitration every tune.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
That is only one factor of cost, and by no means a con-

elusive factor in the case. The least conclusive factor as to value is the matter of the physical property. It is a factor, as pointed out in the report, but it is by no means conclusive as to value. You may have a book value in which the assets are very much greater than the liabilities, but that is by no means a conclusive factor as to what is a fair value for the shares, because the question arises as to what is the actual earning power, the potential earning power, and, apart from that, the financial position of the system. All those factors would have to be taken into consideration. Now, with the procedure before the court, I could well conceive an inquiry on expropriation lasting over a couple of years. My view is that the Board of Arbitrators, selected as set out in this resolution, would be able to deal with the situation very much more expeditiously and just as fairly as before the Exchequer Court.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would that not depend on the scope of the reference of submission to arbitration?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The scope of the reference is a simple one. It reads as follows:
3. The said arbitrators shall determine the value of the said six hundred thousand shares as of the date of the said agreement and the said arbitrators shall proceed in a summary way and may apply their own judgment in determining such value and may receive with respect thereto, such reports and statements authenticated in such way as they may decide and such evidence as they may deem necessary or helpful, examine witnesses under oath and hear the parties by counsel or representatives and that the unanimous determination of the arbitrators shall be final, but should the determination not be unanimous an appeal from such determination shall lie to the Supreme Court of Canada on behalf of the Governor in Council, or of the owners or pledgees, upon any question of law or fact, such appeal to be made within thirty days from the rendering of the determination.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
What is meant by
"summary"? In what way could they proceed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not know any one who knows better than my hon. friend the meaning of the word "summary."
I have a good memory, and so has he. I remember one occasion in the House, when I was called upon to define the word "summary," my hon. friend came to my assistance, as he sometimes does, and he defined the word "summary" in a very satisfactory way. No doubt he will recollect, because no one knows better than he does what it means.
268J

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I know what it means in criminal proceedings, but I don't know about this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I think it denotes freedom from the rigid proceedings of a court, dealing with a matter in a summary or direct eommonsense way, the idea being to obtain an award in a reasonable time.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
"Summary" in legal
phraseology sometimes means that only one party is heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Here we give the power to deal with it in a summary way. My hon. friend from South Renfrew thinks that, instead of determining the value of the shares we should approximate a lump sum in recognition of the services of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. I do not agree with that view at all. I do not believe that it is part of the duty of the Government of Canada, or of Parliament, to recognize the services of men working for their own interests in the building of a transcontinental road or otherwise. I think the proper way to deal with it, if we determine to acquire the shares-as we have to acquire the shares- is to have their fair and reasonable value fixed by arbitration, or by such other procedure as may be determined upon by Parliament.
I think I have traversed the entire ground covered by the hon. member from South Renfrew. I believe that the only information that is not before us and that is required is a statement as to any outstanding liabilities to contractors, and, if possible, a balance sheet for 1917. A balance sheet got out now will not be quite accurate for the reason I have given; it will be a matter of estimate as to the last month or so if the position of the Canadian Northern Railway system is to be shown as of June 30, 1917. It is pointed out to me by he Financial Controller of the Railway Department that on page 8 the amount due contractors is set out as follows:
Due to construction contractors at April 30, 1917, $1,277,323.
These, he tells me, are nearly all holdbacks.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would the minister give us the names of the pledgees of this stock, particularly of the one-sixth which, it is said, is not immediately obtainable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I may be able to obtain that information. The majority of the stock, that is to say, 51 or 52 per cent-I am not in a position to state the

precise percentage-is held by Sir William Mackenzie and' Sir Donald Mann and their pledgees. The one-sixth, about which my hon. friend has inquired, is held, I believe, in England. From time to time in past years certain amounts of that stock were sold or transferred to parties with whom the owners were doing business. I am not positive as to that, however. No doubt the books of the company would show the names of the shareholders, although in the case of scrip stock, the names appearing in the books of the company are not necessarily the names of the owners of the scrip. For instance, Canadian Pacific stock might stand in the name of my hon. friend, but might be transferred by his endorsement to another party. However, I shall endeavour to obtain that information for the House.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: On page 12 of the financial statement the gross earnings of the Canadian Northern Kailway system are given as $42,319,000. Part of that consists of miscellaneous earnings of some subsidiary companies, including interest on investments, etc. Would that include interest upon land stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The financial comptroller of the Railway Department tells me that the interest on the lands is not included in that.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Why does the Government propose to take over certain stock in the Canadian Northern Prairie Lands company and assume thereby liability for the mortgages against the lands amounting to over $21,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The lands of this company were .mortgaged to secure a debenture issue in London. The proceeds of that issue were used in the construction of the road. As the lands weTe sold, their proceeds are available to reduce the mortgage. As the lands are of greater value than the mortgage debt, there would be a substantial equity in those lands when the transaction is complete.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
These lands to which
I refer are unproductive; they are bringing no interest whatever, and they are subject to 'heavy municipal taxes. They are lands the cream of which was selected during the boom days. It is doubtful whether it is advisable to ask this country
10 p.m. to assume a debenture liability of $21,000,000 for something which is in no way connected with the Canadian Northern Railway system. To

leave it in the hands of the present proprietors, the Canadian Northern Prairie Lands company, would be no injustice to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The appraisal of the company is $29,000,000.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is the book value.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
In one sense it
is the book value, but it is also the value placed upon the lands by the company.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Is the Government going to take their valuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I will come to
that in a moment. I do not agree that these lands are not valuable; the best evidence that my hon. friend is wrong is the fact that the land mortgage debentures were floated against them. The land mortgage debentures aggregate some $17,000,000; as against that there is the value of these lands, $29,000,000. My hon. friend says: Why does the Government take over those?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It is more than $17,000,000; it is $21,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We do not take them over directly. On the one side of the balance sheet of the Canadian Northern Railway company are these lands, although they are pledged. On the other side i? the liability of the 'stock issued in respect of them. It would be a very foolish thing for the Government, if they are to become proprietors, to allow the equity in those lands to be lost to the company. My hon. friend would not suggest that the Government should waive the equity in the lands held as security under these land mortgages.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF RESOLUTION RESPECTING CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:

speechtext: How could the Canadian Northern, whose stock the Government is acquiring, divest itself of its bonded indebtedness upon securities issued against this land?

My argument is based upon the fact that the Government should expropriate the railway and rolling stock of the company and nothing more. Leave the company in existence, leave it the stock, and leave it the liabilities.

speechtext: Why does my hon. friend depart from the method which he .suggested a few years ago, when he said that we should acquire the stock by arbitration?

I did not suggest it. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend said that:
It is fair, fair to Mackenzie and Mann and Company and it is a fair and reasonable proposition on behalf of the people of this country.

The amount mentioned was not more than $30,000,000. If it was going to be acquired at all, I suggested that that stipulation should be made. The same argument was made last year. It was argued that, the country having during

past years from time to time come to the rescue of the Canadian Northern, an agreement should be made that, if deemed desirable, it might acquire the stock at an amount not exceeding $30,000,000. Now what I said is that the fact that there is this enormous liability outstanding is a practical argument against taking the property in such a way that the Government would not only acquire the railway and rolling stock, but would- acquire this liability also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was not that enormous liability outstanding then?

I do not know as to that. I take it for granted that the question did not come up. My attention was not called to it at that time, because it was not proposed to take over the stock of the company. It was only proposed to make a loan or give a guarantee. But now it is proposed that the Government shall take over all the stock of the company, and become, in equity and to all intents and purposes, the Canadian Northern Railway company, and, therefore become, ipso facto, liable for all the obligations of the company, including these land grant bonds of $21,000,000.
There is another very strong argument against this proposal for taking over the stock, and it is that it is proposed to do it by arbitration. Perhaps that would be a proper way to proceed if you are simply going to take the stock; but I would ask why, if it is desirable to acquire the Canadian Northern railway and rolling stock, it should not be taken by expropriation in the ordinary way. It used to be the law in this country that whenever the Government expropriated property the valuation was determined by arbitration. That was found to be a very unsatisfactory means of arriving at the value of the property which was expropriated. Favoritism and sympathy entered' into the question of arbitration. The claimant against the Government always had the sympathy of his own arbitrator, because, of course, with respect to him, he would not only have his sympathy but his actual support, and as his arbitrator he would naturally endeavour to get the most he could for the man on whose behalf he was appointed. But it was likewise the case that on the part of the arbitrator appointed to act for the Government there was a feeling of sympathy for the claimant. Then, in the appointment of the third arbitrator, a shrewd clever arbitrator appointed on behalf of the claimant would use his best endeavours' to get a
[Mr. P UK'S lev. j
third arbitrator who would likely be favourable to the claimant. An arbitrator acting for the Government, having the whole nation behind him, is not likely to have the same sympathy for the Government that an arbitrator acting for the claimant would have for the claimant. The reason why that plan was changed was that there was a feeling that arbitrators allowed to claimants against the Government more than ought to have been allowed. That is why the Exchequer Court was established. With a gentleman possessing a knowledge of the law, with experience as to the valuation of property, and utterly impartial- because it was felt that from his judicial position he would be likely to be impartial -and having no sympathy for either the claimant or the Government, it was thought that the Exchequer Court would be a tribunal which would decide these questions equitably as between the individual and the Government. The Exchequer Court has been for many years in operation in Canada, and I have yet to learn that there has been any public dissatisfaction with the manner in which the different judges who have presided over that tribunal from time to time have discharged their duties. Why has that course been departed from in this case? If it is desirable in the public interest to take over the railway property of this company and nothing else-its rolling stock, elevators, and perhaps its hotels- why has the Exchequer Court been passed , over? Why have we reverted to what was the practice forty or fifty years ago, why have we gone back to the proceeding by arbitration as between the claimant and the Government instead of adhering to the practice of submitting a claim of this nature to the Exchequer Court?
There is another objection to this resolution. It does not propose to have the property of this railway system valued. It is not proposed simply to pay for this railway system what it is fairly worth, but the resolution in effect declares that this stock has a value over and above the securities which are against the road. Arbitrators are to be appointed to determine what that value is. Whatever the value is found to be, when the Government takes over the stock at that valuation, it becomes liable for all the securities which are outstanding against -this system and for all the liabilities, whether these liabilities are secured or not.
We find, -Sir, that there is another motive which might influence the arbitrators who may be appointed by the Government and induce them to take a friendly view of the

claim which the Canadian Northern, or Mackenzie and Mann, may put forward for the stock.
It is this. When the bonds of the company to the extent of $45,000,000 were guaranteed under the legislation of 1915, this Government sought to make this House and this country believe that, in taking over $40,000,000 of its common stock, they were getting an asset which would be of value to the country. Else why did they take it? They were not getting a controlling interest; Mackenzie and Mann were left to continue to operate the line and to have its management just as before. They put it forward that it was a stock that might be of viery considerable value to the people of this country. In what position would an arbitrator appointed by this Government ibe if he found 'that the $60,000,000 of stock was of no value? The reproach would be made against the Government which appointed him and whose representatives he would be that the Government of 1915 had simply taken over waste paper as a consideration for entering upon the enormous liability, and that that which the Government then put forward as likely to have a very great value, in the future was practically of no value at all. On the other hand, if the Government arbitrator were to recognize- that the Government were right in assuming that the stock of the company had a value in 1915, he would enable this Government, whose appointee he would be, to say: What foresight we had in 1915; we took ovier, as a consideration for out guarantee, $40,000,00 of stock, and see the three arbitrators have valued $60,000,000 of stock at par, showing that we, in 1915, with that prescience and foresight for which at all times we are prepared to claim credit, got a security worth $40,000,000 as consideration for entering upon this liability.

If he does so, I am prepared to admit that if a proposition had been made then as it is to-day to take over the entire system, I would have said: Take it over by expropriation and let the Exchequer Court determine its value.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
did not say that.

If you took it by expropriation what would be the result? The country would have to pay what the Exchequer Court would find to be the actual value of the property. If you take it by arbitration, take it in the way you propose, no matter whether the country has to pay $10,090,000 or $60,000,000 for the stock, the country becomes liable foir -all the outstanding liabilities of the company, amounting to over - $380,000,000. That is the position in which you are going to. place this -country. The hon. member for Wblland (Mr. German) says it is something over $400,000,000. At all events, it is in that vicinity, and whether the road to-day is worth $200,000,000 or $400,000,000 under this proposition the moment the arbitration is made, the moment the arbitrators finish their work, the Government, under this resolution and under the Bill that is to. be founded upon it, will he obliged in law to take it over and become responsible for all outstanding liabilities of the company. That is the result which will follow the arbitration and, as I have said, if the finding of the arbitrators, is -unanimous, whether it is $10,000,000 or $60,000,000 or more than that, this Government will be bound to pay that amount, without any further authority from this Parliament; they are providing by this resolution that the Government must pay the amount and charge it .against the consolidated revenues of this country.

My hon. friend has said that -there are guaranteed liabilities, that the Dominion has guaranteed $104,000,000 -and the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, have also guaranteed debentures of this company. What are those guaranteed debentures? Those guaranteed by the Dominion amount to $104,000,000, and those guaranteed by -the provinces to $107,000,000, a total of $211,000,000. Assuming that it would 'be in the public interest that these liabilities should be entered into by the Dominion and that Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia should all be saved from their Liabilities, what reason or what excuse is there for passing legislation which will compel this country to assume $147,000,000 of liabilities which are unguaranteed, of liabilities to which the public faith has been in no 'way pledged? What reason is there for that? The investors who took the unguaranteed bonds upon the various sections of the Canadian Northern system had no promise from this Government or from the provincial governments that the -securities would he made good. And yet, irrespective of ihe value of -the securities, this Government is asking Parliament to become liable for this enormous additional sum of $147,000,000 of Unguaranteed securities, and that without any regard whatever to- what amount the investor paid, or to the market value of its -securities. If my hon. friend will take up the financial journals, he will find these unguaranteed securities have no value in the markets of the world of much over fifty per cent, taking one with another. He will find, if he studies the financial journals, and the markets of England, Canada and New York, that he could go and buy these $147,000,000 of securities for somewhere in the vicinity of $70,000,000 to $80,000,000, according to the quoted market value to-day. And of course the securities are based, to a very considerable extent, upon the view which the investors take of the value of the property by which their securities are so secured. Yet to those securities, which I have said are not quoted in the financial market at very much over fifty cents on the dollar, ranging from fifty to sixty, and in some cases seventy per cent, it is proposed to at once give an absolute value, by the Government going behind them and taking the place of the Canadian Northern. I do not think that is a fair proposition. It seems to me that what ought to he done is for the Government to expropriate this property, to have the various portions of the system, so far as these portions are 
covered by independent securities, valued by the Exchequer Court, have them disposed of, and, if the holders of the securities will not make the necessary arrangement, dispose of the property, and divide the assets according to the priorities and according to the claims of the various security holders. But, without any evidence whatever of the actual cost, and knowing that the actual value as- represented by the earnings is not sufficient to cover what it is proposed to pay, why the Government should undertake to pledge the credit of the country, not only for what may be awarded to Mackenzie and Mann as the holders of the common stock, but also to meet the necessary liabilities up to their face value, passes my comprehension. It seems to me it is a proposal which should not commend itself to the people of this country.	And it is proposed
to assume this enormous liability, which will run u.p to somewhere in the vicinity of $500,000,000, at -a time when, in consequence of this war and in consequence of the markets of England being clo-sed to the Canadian Government, Canada is obliged to strain every nerve to borrow the money for the purpose of -doing her part in connection with the world conflict. The minister proposes to do this at -a time when he is obliged to forget his determination and the -determination of the people with whom he was acting not long ago, when they cried out: "No truck or trade with the Yankees," -and to go to -the New York money market and pay the very high rate of interest of six per cent for a shortterm loan extending over -a period of two years. This Government's credit has been strained to such a -point that Canada, with all its vast resources, with its wonderful possibilities of future development, with its enormous riche-s, is compelled to pay two -and a half per cent more in the markets of the United States than -the United States Government was obliged to pay in connection with the flotation of its Liberty Loan, amounting to some $3,000,000,000. Is that a good record for this Government, and is this a good time in which to further strain the credit of the country, -and to incur this enormous obligation, of, as I have said, in the vicinity of half a billion dollars?

p-ay double the value of a property in order to get extended credit -who is willing to pay $500,000,000 to-day for a property that I do not believe the Exchequer Court would value at a figure upwards of $300,000,000.

would be $18,000,000 a year. As it stands now the security of the company will average about three and a half per cent on $400,000,000. The reason that these securities are only worth half their face value today-

I am asking a question.

It is particularly trying to my hon. friend, who speaks so little and is so very free in his remarks, to have to wait till I get through, having made up his mind he ought to speak on this question.
I thought the hon. gentleman had given me his place.

I am not through yet. I did not say that we would pay $300,000,000 for the property by expropriation, but what I say is that, having reference to the system, to the mileage, the mode in which it has been constructed, and the report of these commissioners, I doubt very much whether the Exchequer Court will allow more than $300,000,000, for this entire property.
When you consider the valuation put upon the property of the Canadian Pacific and the superiority of its construction over that of the Canadian Northern, you realize that the Exchequer Court would hardly value the Canadian Northern property at upwards of $300,000,000. But the Minister of Finance says: Even though the property may be worth only $300,000,000; even though there are $147,000,000 of unguaranteed debentures outstanding which in the markets of the world are not worth more than fifty or sixty cents on the dollar, these bonds have quite a long time to run and it is better for us to buy than to be obliged to pay cash foT the property. they are called upon to pay, of about $2,000,000. If they were able to do that a year ago, what is to hinder them, with their present rolling stock and equipment, from handling the grain business otf the West fairly well during the coming year? Nothing that I can see. I am told that the Canadian Northern has given a very satis-faetbry service in the West, and there are many parts of this country where the service given by the railroads is not at all as satisfactory to the people who ought to be served by those roads as the service given by the Canadian Northern and the various branches of the system in the section of the country through which it runs. As long ago as the year 1911, the Prime Minister authorized Mr. Fowler, who has until lately represented the constituency of Kings and Alibert, and who is now a member of the Senate, to declare to the people of New Brunswick in effect that if the Conservative party came into power, it would take hold of all the branch lines of the Intercolonial and make them a part of the Intercolonial system.
That message was communicated to the people of New Brunswick, who were deeply interested in this question of railway accommodation, and no doubt it had considerable effect upon the people, because they relied on the statements which were made. Yet from that day to this, with only two exceptions, the people have seen those promises, unfulfilled; they have seen nothing done to ensure better accommodation for the people of the province so far as the branch lines, connecting with the Intercolonial are concerned. What am I to say to these people, and what are the representatives of that province to say to them, when this enormous liability is imposed upon the country?-a burden which they are to bear in common with the rest of the people. They will say: Before incurring these new obligations the Government ought to carry out the pledges which they have made to the people of a section of Canada which is not less important than the sections of the country through which the Canadian Northern system runs.

Just a word with regard to what my hon. friend says as to the fact that now is the best time to buy the railroad because the securities were floated at a low rate of interest. All other things being equal, that might be so, but I would point my hon. friend to the remark which he made in 1916 when it was proposed to lend to the Canadian Northern the sum of $15,000,000. My hon. friend then referred to the facts that in this war, which had been going on much longer than was ever anticipated, Canada had been obliged to borrow large sums of money, and that our expenditure was running up to about $900,000 per day. He said that that was not the time to engage upon new liabilities. I ask him to remember that statement to-day. Surely the time is no more opportune to-day than it was a year ago. I think that the people of this country will regard this proposal as a most improvident one. There may be a question whether any time it would be desirable to enter upon the system of government ownership; but this is not the occasion when the country should be committed to an obligation so vast in its character and so uncertain in its results as this proposal involves, nor is this the mode in which so great a change should be presented.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been engaged for about an hour and a half in showing that he did not know what he was talking about in 1914 and 1916. He distinctly advocated on three or four occasions in 1914 the acquisition of the stock of the Cauadian Northern railway by arbitration, and in no ether way. He is proceeding to demonstrate now, to his own satisfaction if not to the satisfaction of any one else, that to acquire that stock by arbitration is a most improvident method, and absolutely against the best interests of the people of this country. He has told us that arbitration was discarded forty or fifty years ago. Might I ask him, then, why he advocated it in 1914 and in 1916 for this very purpose? Were those considerations which he has so eloquently expressed at very great length this evening entirely absent from his mind on that occasion? What is the reason that he regarded the proposal to acquire the stock by arbitration as an eminently wise and reasonable one in 1914 and again in 1916, and that he spends an hour and a half this evening in demonstrating that any such proposal is absolutely absurd and entirely opposed to the public interest? My hon.

friend has taken a long time to explain himself, and I think he will require a much longer time before he convinces the committee that there is really anything in his explanation.
Then he says that the mere suggestion of arbitration puts a value upon the stock. He did much more than that in 1914, when he suggested a value of $30,000,000 for the stock. We have done no such thing on this occasion. We have simply left it to the arbitrators to determine what the value of the stock is. If they consider it of no value, they will find accordingly; if they *consider it of some value, they will find accordingly. We do not suggest to the arbitrators, as he proposed to do, and did do in 1914, that the stock might have a maximum value of $30,000,000.
Then he says that a proposal of this kind gives value to the unguaranteed bonds. If the value is affected by this proposal did not his proposal of 1914 and of 1916 effect precisely the same purpose? What is the distinction which the hon. gentleman draws in his own favour between a proposal to acquire by arbitration the stock of this railway at a maximum value of $30,000,000, and a proposal to acquire $60,000,000 now without suggesting any such value as he then named? I am bound to say that I have followed the hon. gentleman with a great deal of attention, and I still adhere to the opinion I expressed a little while .ago, that it will be necessary for him to occupy the time of this committee and of this House at ,a very much greater length than he has done this evening if he wishes to make us understand the supposed distinction between the arbitration which he proposed in 1914, and the proposal which the Government makes at this time.
As far as the additional cost of completing the road, is concerned, and as far as the liabilities outstanding against the road are concerned, it must be perfectly obvious to any one that the arbitrators, when they come to determine the value of the stock, will have to take into account those considerations, and therefore it seems to me that he is merely wasting the time of the committee when he dwells at great length upon such matters. He started out with a proposal respecting the land bonds. Up to the present I am not at all clear as to what he means. The proceeds, of the land bonds went into the construction of this road, and therefore they are properly to be taken into account, I suppose, as part of the cost of this road. Does he suggest,
as I inquired before-although I have not obtained any -satisfactory answer-that that part of the cost of the road should be omitted? If he -agrees that it should not be omitted, iwhy does he suggest that the land against which these bonds were issued *should be eliminated from the assets of this system?

What I say is this. The investor who put his money in those bonds had nothing to do with what was done with the proceeds. The investor lent his money on the security of the land. I would eliminate both. I would neither assume the liability nor take the land.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a most extraordinary proposition. The proceeds of these bonds have gone into the construction of the road. If there had not been any lien to secure them at all how could you omit them from the cost of the road? The money was spent, and is represented in the road today. What he suggests, if he suggests anything at all, is that we should omit from the assets of this system, the land upon which those bonds are secured. Surely he must realize upon reflection that that is not a suggestion which is in the interests of the people of this country. Further than that, so far as all these assets and liabilities are concerned, they must be taken into account by the arbitrators when they come to determine the value of the stock, if it has any value. Therefore all the argument which my hon. friend has poured forth in such volume to the committee this evening does not seem to have any relevancy to the debate at all. The money went into the road, and therefore must be taken into account. Why, in the name of all that is reasonable, should we omit the -land upon which that money was raised?
I must confess, although I followed my hon. friend with the greatest possible attention, that I am utterly unable to see any common sense-if I may be permitted to say so without any desire to be offensive 

in the suggestion he made.
However, it is perfectly obvious that we cannot get the resolution through to-night. My hon. friend will have an opportunity of making any further explanation that he desires to-morrow, and I shall move now that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

There is a provision for default in the statute of 1914, section 21. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if the Canadian Northern has made default and if the penalty provided by

subsection (a) of section 21 of the statute of 1914, under the provisions of the new trust deed, has been exacted. I would ask the minister if he would produce the trust deed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Has there been any default under the provisions of- that trust deed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Canadian Northern has not, so far as I am aware, defaulted on any of its securities. But
my hon. friend knows that financial aid is required, and will be required each year, to prevent default. We will be glad to bring down a copy of the trust mortgage, which was executed in 1914-and which I think has been laid on the Table once or twice during the last two years-and any other information that my hon. friends desire.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 11.30 p.m.
